consensus: The scientific community should adapt by treating AI as a research tool governed by clear rules, not as an author or a substitute for scholarly judgment. Journals, universities, and funders should adopt transparent policies requiring disclosure of how AI was used in analysis, writing, and literature review. Research training should include AI literacy, especially the verification of outputs, since AI systems can fabricate references and produce plausible but incorrect claims. Peer review and research integrity procedures should be strengthened to cope with the growing volume of low-quality, AI-generated text. Researcher evaluation should reward originality, methodological rigor, and real contributions to knowledge rather than publication counts. Finally, accountability must remain with humans: researchers are responsible for the validity, ethics, and interpretation of their findings. In education research, this also means studying how AI affects learning and teacher preparation, not only using it as a tool.
comment: I would like to emphasize that the impact of AI on research will differ across fields and regions. In education research, much depends on context: classroom practice, teacher preparation, and local languages and curricula. AI tools perform less reliably in lower-resourced languages such as Uzbek, so researchers working in these contexts need to verify AI outputs especially carefully. I also believe that access to AI tools and to training in their responsible use should be equitable, so that the gap between well-resourced and less-resourced research communities does not widen. Finally, since pre-service teachers will shape how the next generation uses AI, teacher education programs deserve particular attention in discussions about AI and the future of research and education.

consensus:
Let me be blunt: the polite consensus that "AI is just a tool, embrace it wisely" avoids the real question. The substitutive pressure AI exerts on academic work is not exaggerated; it is structural. Literature reviews, data cleaning, code writing, manuscript polishing, even peer-review drafting: these tasks, which once consumed most of a researcher's working hours, can now be delegated to a model in minutes. A community that responds to this with slogans about "human-AI collaboration" is refusing to name what is actually happening.
But honesty cuts both ways. If we look at what these models actually produce, the picture is far less impressive. Current AI output is, at its core, recombination: statistically plausible stitching of what already exists in the training data. It frequently lacks logical coherence across longer arguments, fabricates references with confident fluency, and cannot tell a true claim from a well-phrased false one. It generates text that looks like scholarship without doing the work of scholarship. Calling this "research assistance" flatters it; much of it is content filler with no epistemic value.
Here we should recall how research actually begins. Discovery starts with doubt. Only because we first question an existing claim, distrust a convenient explanation, or refuse to accept a result at face value, do we have anything worth researching at all. Doubt is not an obstacle to science; it is its origin. And this is precisely what AI does not possess. What the machine offers is mechanical capability: retrieval, recombination, pattern completion. What the human researcher offers is the capacity to be unconvinced. These are not the same kind of thing, and the community should stop treating them as interchangeable.
So the adaptation should follow from both facts at once:
First, stop outsourcing judgment. AI can substitute for the production of academic text, but not for the verification of claims. The scarcest resource in science was never words; it is warranted belief. Any use of AI that bypasses human verification of logic, data, and sources should be treated as misconduct, not as efficiency.
Second, redefine what counts as valuable work. If a task can be fully delegated to a model, then that task was already mechanical, and it should no longer confer academic credit. Evaluation systems must shift weight toward what AI demonstrably cannot do: posing genuinely new questions, producing original empirical data, and taking responsibility for the truth of a claim.
Third, let humans be liberated from the mechanical, not compete with it. The point of offloading routine work to machines is to free researchers for the irreducibly human parts of science: doubt, curiosity, judgment, and the willingness to say the established view is wrong. A researcher who uses AI to produce more text has learned nothing. A researcher who uses the freed time to think more skeptically has adapted correctly.
The bottom line: AI will absorb the mechanical layer of academic work, and pretending otherwise is self-deception. But a community that mistakes fluent recombination for knowledge, and lets it into the literature unchecked, has not adapted to AI; it has surrendered to it.

Ultimately, the competitive advantage of the scientific community will not lie in its ability to use AI to produce more publications, but in its ability to use AI to produce better science.

I would also emphasise one important point: AI will not necessarily make scientific researchers less important. On the contrary, it may make their expertise, originality, critical judgement and ethical responsibility even more valuable.

The future of science should therefore be neither science without AI nor science governed by AI, but science strengthened by AI and guided by human intelligence, scientific integrity and responsibility.

Overall, AI should be used as a tool to support scientific research, rather than replace human knowledge, critical thinking and scientific judgement.

future_5_TEXT: My long-term strategy is to integrate AI into my research and professional work while concentrating on areas where human judgement, strategic understanding and institutional accountability remain indispensable.Through Aquarian Systematic Resilience (ASR), I intend to develop governance architectures and analytical frameworks that address the risks arising when AI systems increasingly influence or undertake decisions within complex, interconnected infrastructures. This includes examining the distinction between technical capability and legitimate authority, establishing boundaries for delegated autonomy, and ensuring that human oversight, intervention and accountability remain effective.I also intend to use AI to enhance research efficiency, literature analysis, scenario modelling, comparative case studies and the development of new analytical methods. However, I believe that the ability to generate information or analytical outputs should not be confused with the ability to establish their validity, interpret their wider implications or assume responsibility for consequential decisions.In the long term, my focus will be on combining AI-enabled analytical capabilities with interdisciplinary research, independent critical thinking and practical governance principles. Rather than competing with AI in areas it can increasingly automate, I aim to concentrate on designing the frameworks through which humans and intelligent systems can work together safely, responsibly and effectively.
consensus:
The scientific community should adapt by developing a clear governance framework for the responsible integration of AI into research. This requires moving beyond the traditional question of whether AI can assist researchers towards addressing how much independence it should be granted, under what conditions, and with what accountability.

AI can significantly enhance literature reviews, data analysis, modelling, hypothesis generation and interdisciplinary collaboration. However, its outputs must remain subject to scientific scrutiny, independent verification and reproducibility. Researchers should be transparent about AI's contribution, retain responsibility for their findings, and distinguish machine-generated analysis from validated scientific evidence.

More importantly, institutions should establish boundaries for delegated AI authority, including mechanisms for human oversight, intervention and withdrawal of autonomy. Scientific integrity, ethical responsibility and accountability cannot simply be delegated to algorithms.

The community should also invest in AI literacy, interdisciplinary collaboration and updated research standards. Ultimately, the objective should not be to restrict AI's contribution or embrace unrestricted automation, but to establish a balanced research ecosystem in which AI expands scientific capability while human judgement, intellectual independence and institutional accountability remain fundamental.
comment:
The scientific community should treat AI governance as an integral part of research, not merely an ethical or regulatory consideration. 
As AI becomes more autonomous, clear boundaries, human oversight, intervention mechanisms and accountability must ensure that technical capability does not automatically confer decision-making authority. Ultimately, AI should expand scientific discovery while preserving intellectual independence, research integrity and human responsibility.

AI systems should be allowed substantial operational autonomy in research tasks where their outputs can be independently verified. However, scientific accountability, the evaluation of theoretical contributions, and decisions with institutional or ethical consequences must remain subject to meaningful human oversight.

Research institutions should develop transparent standards for documenting AI involvement, strengthen methodological training, and prioritise the reproducibility and critical evaluation of AI-assisted findings. Academic assessment should place greater emphasis on the originality of research questions, explanatory value, methodological validity, and robustness of evidence rather than publication volume.

The central challenge is not to restrict AI autonomy indiscriminately, but to establish governance mechanisms that distinguish technological capability from epistemic reliability and institutional responsibility.
comment:
I believe the survey places too much emphasis on predicting whether and when AI will replace human researchers, rather than examining how human–AI collaboration can be organised to improve scientific research.

The central issue is not technological competition between humans and AI, but the conditions under which their interaction produces better research outcomes. In my experience, AI already substantially reduces the time and effort required for analytical work, programming, academic writing, and the preparation of educational materials. However, the frequency of AI use tells us little about a researcher's ability to evaluate the reliability, limitations, and scientific value of AI-generated results.

Researchers differ considerably in their digital competencies, methodological expertise, and capacity to use AI critically. Academic rank is not a reliable substitute for these characteristics. Consequently, aggregating expectations about AI's future capabilities may reveal prevailing attitudes, but cannot establish which forms of human–AI collaboration are scientifically productive.

I would encourage future research to examine how researchers' competencies, task characteristics, levels of AI autonomy, and verification practices jointly influence research quality, originality, and productivity.

future_5_TEXT: In my view, when thinking about a long-term strategy for responding to the development of artificial intelligence, we should start with education. I believe that media literacy, including education about AI, should be a compulsory part of learning at every level, from primary school to university. This is not simply about teaching young people how to use new tools or different generative AI models. More importantly, it is about helping them understand how these technologies work, what opportunities they offer, and what risks they may bring. Young people should learn to critically evaluate the information they receive, recognise manipulation, check the reliability of sources, and understand that AI can also make mistakes. However, we cannot achieve this without properly preparing teachers. That is why it is equally important to provide them with training and practical support, while gradually adapting educational curricula to a changing world. I am convinced that our greatest challenge will not be simply keeping up with the rapid development of artificial intelligence, but preparing people to live in a world where AI is becoming increasingly present. We need to learn how to use these technologies without losing our ability to think independently, ask questions, and make our own decisions. Artificial intelligence should help us think, not think for us. And this, in my opinion, should be the foundation of our long-term educational strategy.
consensus:
In my opinion, the scientific community should closely follow developments in artificial intelligence and continuously improve its ability to use these technologies in an informed, critical and responsible way. AI is already changing how we conduct research, analyse data and prepare scientific publications. We cannot simply ignore these changes or see them only as a threat. At the same time, we need to maintain a healthy level of scepticism about both the potential and the limitations of these technologies. It is particularly important to uphold the principles of scientific integrity, transparency and responsibility for our own research findings.
I also believe that the academic community should actively participate in developing guidelines for the use of AI in research, rather than simply adapting to solutions offered by technology companies. Artificial intelligence can be an extremely useful tool in scientific work, but it should never replace independent thinking, critical reflection or researchers' responsibility for their own work.

AI has enormous potential to accelerate scientific discovery, improve data analysis, and support interdisciplinary research. However, transparency, reproducibility, independent validation of AI-generated results, and human accountability must remain fundamental principles.

Ultimately, the scientific community should evaluate AI not only in terms of efficiency and productivity, but also in terms of scientific quality, originality, trustworthiness, and its contribution to addressing real-world challenges.

AI offers considerable opportunities to accelerate data analysis, literature reviews, scientific writing, research planning, and administrative processes. consensus:
The scientific community should actively embrace the opportunities offered by AI while developing appropriate standards to ensure scientific integrity, transparency, and reproducibility. AI has considerable potential to accelerate scientific discovery through advanced data analysis, modelling, literature synthesis, and the integration of multidisciplinary information. However, its application must be accompanied by critical evaluation of AI-generated results and clear accountability for scientific conclusions.

Research institutions, universities, funding agencies, and scientific publishers should establish transparent guidelines for responsible AI use, including disclosure requirements, data protection, authorship policies, and mechanisms for identifying errors, biases, and fabricated information. Scientific education should increasingly incorporate AI literacy, enabling researchers to use these tools effectively without compromising independent reasoning and methodological rigour.

Importantly, the scientific community should reconsider how research quality is assessed. As AI makes scientific writing and routine analytical tasks increasingly efficient, greater emphasis should be placed on the originality of research questions, methodological innovation, robustness of evidence, and genuine scientific contributions rather than publication volume.

Ultimately, AI should be regarded as an instrument for enhancing human scientific creativity and discovery, not replacing intellectual independence, critical thinking, or scientific responsibility. Ensuring equitable access to AI technologies across institutions and countries will also be essential to prevent widening disparities within the global research community.

High standards for manuscript handling carried out entirely by humans must be maintained, with AI used exclusively for refining language, style, and grammar. Furthermore, the current framework should shift toward more traditional, rigorous methods. For instance, requiring authors to provide a screen-recorded video of the entire writing process from start to finish would help. Additionally, ensuring that figures, tables, and images are not AI-generated, and employing blockchain-based software to "sign" the document (verifying that the text was written manually rather than copied and pasted from an AI tool), would help mitigate the unethical use of AI in content creation. Much of the unethical use of AI stems from the vast disparities in working conditions within the research field. As AI continues to advance and become more precise while the labor landscape for researchers remains deeply unequal the unchecked use of AI will likely increase. Researchers may turn to it to boost their publication statistics and metrics to meet the demands of their positions, while those seeking such roles may increasingly rely on it to improve their chances of securing a position. Implementing measures like those mentioned above would help curb the unethical use of AI.
consensus:
Publishing houses must adapt and modernize their bureaucratic management systems, as the wait for a response regarding a submitted article can currently span months or even years. Furthermore, the process should be more thoroughly globalized, and funding models must be made transparent and equitable for all parties involved. A new system for manuscripts or applied projects should be established one that requires proof of human authorship such as "feasible project" articles. 

There should also be a greater emphasis on qualitative research and mixed-methods studies that incorporate complexity theory, as these necessitate human insight and complex thinking. While research in the exact and basic sciences (rooted in the quantitative-positivist paradigm) will be the most significantly affected, qualitative approaches and the rigorous standards applied to them must also be expanded within these fields. 

Measures should be adopted that rely entirely on the researcher rather than on the potential for AI to generate the content. For instance, this could involve specialized software that records the user's screen, utilizes blockchain-based digital signatures for the text and the document, and restricts "copy-paste" functions allowing only for the inclusion of direct quotations (whether long or short). 

Additionally, the process could involve four witnesses: two individuals external to the peer-review process, and two others tasked with supervising those witnesses by observing, in real time, the researcher as they draft or manage the article. consensus:
I believe the scientific community should adapt to recent advances in AI, but should not regard AI as a replacement for human researchers.

At present, AI performs particularly well in fields where problems have clearly defined boundaries, explicit rules and measurable outcomes, such as mathematics and certain computational sciences. However, its reasoning remains relatively constrained. It can identify patterns, process large amounts of information and optimise solutions within a given framework, but it is less capable of questioning the framework itself or recognising important factors that have not been adequately represented in the available data.

This limitation is particularly relevant to medicine. Clinical problems are inherently multidimensional, involving biological variability, patient characteristics, treatment responses and contextual factors that are often difficult to quantify. Many clinical decisions take place in areas where the boundaries between different conditions and outcomes are not clearly defined. In such settings, AI may provide useful analytical support, but its conclusions still require interpretation and critical judgement by experienced researchers and clinicians.

Therefore, I believe the scientific community should embrace AI as a research tool rather than treat it as an independent scientific authority. Researchers should learn to use AI to improve efficiency, explore hypotheses and analyse complex datasets, while retaining responsibility for defining research questions, evaluating evidence and interpreting findings. Ultimately, scientific progress requires not only the ability to find answers, but also the ability to recognise which questions are worth asking.
comment: I believe the most important consideration is to maintain a balance between embracing technological progress and preserving independent scientific thinking. AI can substantially improve research efficiency, but scientific innovation should not become merely an exercise in using increasingly powerful tools. The ability to identify meaningful questions, challenge existing assumptions and interpret findings in their broader clinical and scientific context remains essential. The scientific community should therefore promote the responsible use of AI while ensuring that human judgement, scientific integrity and critical thinking remain at the centre of research.

future_5_TEXT: My long-term strategy is to integrate AI more deeply into my research while strengthening the skills that remain essential to rigorous scientific inquiry. I aim to use AI to support computational modeling, data analysis, literature review, and methodological exploration, while maintaining human responsibility for research questions, critical interpretation, ethical decisions, and scientific validation.I also intend to expand my research on human-AI interaction, particularly how AI autonomy, transparency, and human control influence the production and evaluation of knowledge. consensus:
The scientific community should move beyond treating AI merely as a productivity tool and develop clear frameworks for its responsible integration into research. This requires establishing standards for transparency, reproducibility, independent validation, and accountability, particularly when AI systems contribute autonomously to scientific findings.

Research institutions, journals, and funding agencies should reconsider how scientific contributions are evaluated, placing greater emphasis on methodological rigor, originality, and the reliability of evidence rather than publication volume. AI autonomy should be proportional to the risks and consequences of each task, with human oversight remaining essential for ethical judgments and consequential decisions.

Equally important, universities should strengthen researchers' AI literacy and critical thinking while ensuring equitable access to these technologies. The goal should not simply be faster scientific production, but more trustworthy, inclusive, and socially meaningful knowledge.
comment:
One important consideration is that increasing AI autonomy in scientific research should not automatically be equated with scientific progress. The ability to generate results must be accompanied by independent verification, methodological transparency, and clear accountability.

I also believe that the scientific community should pay greater attention to how AI changes the role of researchers, particularly their capacity to formulate meaningful questions, critically evaluate evidence, and exercise scientific judgment.

Finally, from the perspective of researchers working in Latin America, equitable access to advanced AI systems is a significant concern. Without appropriate institutional support and international collaboration, these technologies could reinforce existing inequalities in global knowledge production.

The central challenge is not simply determining how much autonomy AI can achieve, but deciding how much autonomy science should responsibly grant it.

1. Transform Research Methods

However, this adaptation must be accompanied by clear ethical guidelines, transparency, and responsible use to protect research integrity and prevent issues such as fabricated references, biased results, and plagiarism. Universities and research institutions should also invest in AI education, training programmes, and interdisciplinary collaborations to prepare researchers and students for the evolving scientific landscape. Ultimately, AI should be considered a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human expertise, critical thinking, creativity, and scientific judgment. The scientific community must therefore find a balance between technological innovation and the fundamental principles of rigorous, ethical, and evidence-based research.

comment: Using LLM models for writing academic papers still presents challenges. While they excel at correcting the grammar of individual sentences, they struggle to develop a coherent narrative that flows logically throughout the entire text. Instead of fully exploring one topic before moving on to the next, these models often jump between ideas in a disorganized fashion, resulting in wordy, convoluted prose where the overall flow frequently breaks down. Although some early issues—such as the use of vocabulary rarely found in academic papers—have been largely addressed, current commercialized models are not yet suitable as fully autonomous writing tools. It would be highly beneficial if these limitations were overcome, or if specialized tools designed specifically for scientific writing were developed.

future_5_TEXT: My situation is a little unusual because I plan to retire from my faculty position in mid-2027, so “long term” for me means two things: what I leave behind in my program, and what I do afterward through my consulting and writing.For the program, my strategy is to make sure our graduates can use AI competently and ethically before they ever walk into a school. That means building AI literacy into coursework, teaching students to treat AI as a thinking partner rather than an answer machine, and being honest with them about its limits around confidentiality, bias, and accuracy. School counselors are already being handed these tools, often without guidance, and I’d rather my students learn the judgment here than on the job with real kids.For my own work, I’m leaning in rather than waiting it out. Counseling technology has been one of my scholarship areas for decades, and AI is the biggest shift I’ve seen in that space. I’m writing and presenting on AI in school counseling, offering workshops to state associations, and using AI daily in my own work for drafting, feedback, data analysis, and research. My view is that the parts of counseling that matter most (relationships, presence, ethical judgment, advocacy) aren’t going away, but the administrative and data work around them is changing fast. Counselors who figure out how to offload that work to AI will have more time for students. Those who don’t will fall behind, and the profession risks having these decisions made for it by vendors and administrators.The risk I see is overreliance: students and practitioners who let AI do the thinking instead of sharpening it. So my strategy is to model the opposite, using it heavily but critically, and to keep saying out loud where it falls short.
consensus:
Yes, and faster than it currently is. Most of the scientific community is still treating AI as a policy problem to be contained rather than a tool that has already changed how research gets done. Journals are writing disclosure rules while many authors are quietly using AI anyway, which creates a gap between stated norms and actual practice. That gap is the real problem.

A few things I think need to happen. First, disclosure standards should be specific and practical, saying what was used and for what (literature searching, coding qualitative data, drafting, editing), rather than a vague checkbox. Second, peer review needs to adapt. Reviewers are already stretched thin, and AI makes it easy to produce polished manuscripts with weak substance, so journals will need better ways to evaluate rigor and not just readability. Third, we have to train graduate students and early-career researchers to use AI critically. They will use it either way; the question is whether they learn to verify its output, recognize fabricated citations, and keep their own thinking in the driver’s seat.

In my own field, counseling and counselor education, there’s an added layer. Our research often involves sensitive data about minors, and researchers need clear guidance on what can and cannot go into AI tools without violating confidentiality or IRB protocols. Right now that guidance is thin.

The opportunity is real too. AI can make research more accessible to practitioners, help with data analysis that used to require specialized training, and speed up the slow parts of scholarship. But that only helps if the community holds onto its standards for honesty, transparency, and human accountability. AI can assist the work. It can’t be the one responsible for it.

future_5_TEXT: I believe it is important to stay up to date on the use of artificial intelligence, its different applications, and which tools we can use for each activity. I don't think AI is entirely bad if we know how to use it properly. We should not delegate all our reasoning to it, but we can certainly take advantage of it to strengthen our ideas and improve our work.As we know, AI systems learn from the information we provide them. It is like a child who learns and behaves according to the information they receive. In the end, we are the ones who have control over how and for what purposes we use these tools.Therefore, I believe that if we stay up to date on how artificial intelligence can support us in each area of our work, we will be able to take advantage of its benefits and adapt to changes rather than seeing it as a tool that could replace us.
consensus:
I believe the scientific community should start researching and learning about prompt engineering in order to understand how to formulate questions correctly when using AI and obtain more accurate and useful information. We know that we can ask AI almost anything and receive an answer, but that does not necessarily mean the answer is correct, as it may depend on the context, time, location, information sources, or even the region we are considering.

Nowadays, it is not just about verifying information through Google Scholar, Dialnet, SciELO, or other scientific journals that allow us to validate information and cite sources correctly. We should also look for alternatives to learn how to extract useful, specific, and verifiable information from artificial intelligence, avoiding overly generic answers.

I believe we should explore AI tools specifically designed for scientific research, which can facilitate this process without replacing the rigor, analysis, and critical thinking of researchers.
comment:
I believe we are at a point where we must learn to adapt to changes and not be afraid of new technologies. Artificial intelligence has arrived to transform many of the activities we carry out, including education and scientific research. However, I believe the challenge is not only learning how to use it, but also regulating its use and establishing clear guidelines on how, when, and for what purposes we can use it.

In our country, as well as within our institutions, there are still many questions about to what extent the use of AI is permitted and which activities it can be incorporated into. Therefore, I believe we should not rely solely on developing our own research, but should also seek guidance from the authorities responsible for higher education, IT specialists, international organizations such as UNESCO, and different academic networks that can provide us with a basic framework or reference guidelines.

This would allow us to establish criteria for implementing these tools in our academic work, research, teaching, and also in our students' learning processes. We must not lose our ability to question, analyze, create, and think for ourselves. Technology is constantly advancing, but our human ability to reason, make decisions, and generate knowledge remains essential.

Rather than seeing AI as a threat, we should see it as an opportunity to learn, innovate, and grow professionally, but always through responsible, ethical, and regulated use.

future_5_TEXT: AI seems to have a tendency to transform difficult technical challenges which relied on human intuition for progress into search problems over solutions to technical problems. In my field of computational chemistry, I can now give AI access to tools which already existed and it can competently execute any series of simulations I request. In the past, deciding what simulations to run to answer some chemical question was dictated by my own familiarity with the simulation methods and my understanding of the problem in question. Now, AI can try every possible simulation strategy over a huge number of chemical systems. Some of these simulations will yield useful insights and some will not. This is analogous to AI being presented open problems in math and generating proofs, proofs of a weaker problem, or making no progress at all. It is then up to the human to carry out an informed search over the results to condense the outcomes into human understanding and direct future work towards questions of interest to humans.Given that, the strategy I am taking is to shift my research toward areas where broad exploration, carried out by AI, followed by compression of those results into human-comprehensible principles is possible. Specifically, nearly all types of design problem fit this mold. Searching for chemical reactions with special properties, designing molecules which have an affinity for a protein or surface, designing catalysts to accelerate certain reactions, etc. These types of searches over the space of molecules used to be done more or less by intuition. We can now more or less us brute force and then have humans carry out searches over the data and iterate with the AI on this process.One should always ask the question of whether or not AI will eventually be able to fill any role played humans in scientific research, especially computational scientific research. It seems to me that the selection of scientific research questions is a matter of taste which is dictated by the present needs of humans combined with the questions which we believe to solvable in a relatively short period of time. I have no doubt that AI will become better at this type of judgment which depends on human social factors, but this is a type of fuzzy reasoning which AI will struggle with simply but I expect progress at this type of task to be slow simply because it is ill-defined and progress is hard to verify. So, the aforementioned search problems seem stable as a human pursuit because the "right" places to look are contingent on social factors which are not readily available to AIs and change for capricious reasons.
consensus: We should dramatically raise the standards for publication. We should begin aggregating repositories of mostly-AI-generated results which are a sort of feedstock for creating comprehensible scientific theories. We should encourage more scientists to function as generalists who work in an interdisciplinary manner. As an example, I could likely write a few paragraphs describing exactly the sets of simulations an AI should carry out for every research paper I have ever published and it would be able to reproduce all of the data in those papers. At the time, many of these types of simulations were non-trivial to carry out so the insights derived from them were valuable to the scientific community. The need for that type of very niche expertise has been obviated away by AI. This means that was once publishable and respectable scientific research is now trivially carried out if sufficient computing resources are available. This type of work is, therefore, not worthy of publishing in a scientific journal. The data itself is valuable and should therefore be canonicalized in some kind of open database. Given that non-specialists can now carry out specialist tasks, it seems to me the inevitable response is that humans will become scientific generalists except for those exceptionally talented specialists who, in a certain sense, form the frontier of expertise which AIs will eventually be able to emulate.

future_5_TEXT: I am increasingly integrating AI into my training and development work with researchers, helping them understand not just how to use emerging tools, but how to exercise critical judgement about when, why and whether to use them. This includes exploring the implications for research practices, professional development, interdisciplinary collaboration and the skills researchers will need in the future.Over the longer term, I see opportunities to develop this work further, particularly around responsible AI use, research culture and the environmental sustainability of AI. I am also exploring how AI can support my own applied research, including evidence reviews, policy analysis and the synthesis of interdisciplinary material, while retaining human oversight, critical interpretation and accountability.My strategy is to focus less focused on learning lots of individual AI tools and more on developing the expertise needed to evaluate their use and integrate them thoughtfully into research and professional practice. consensus:
The scientific community needs to respond to AI developments in ways that go beyond technical training or the adoption of new tools. I would highlight four priorities:

Embed critical AI literacy into researcher development. Researchers at all career stages need opportunities to experiment with AI, understand its capabilities and limitations, and develop the judgement to decide when its use is appropriate. This should be integrated into wider researcher development rather than treated as a standalone technical skill.

Rethink research skills and professional development. Scientific institutions need clear expectations around the responsible use of AI, including transparency, reproducibility, research integrity and meaningful human oversight. Researchers should be actively involved in shaping these approaches rather than simply complying with centrally determined policies.

The scientific community needs to consider environmental costs, inequalities in access, commercial dependencies and the implications for public trust in research. Decisions about AI use should be informed by its wider costs and benefits, not simply potential efficiency gains.

future_5_TEXT: My long-term strategy is to integrate artificial intelligence into my research while maintaining human responsibility, scientific rigor, and ethical oversight. As an educational researcher, I intend to strengthen my work on the ethical governance of generative AI, educational leadership, and public policy, particularly regarding its implications for educational institutions and knowledge production.I plan to expand the use of AI for literature reviews, data analysis, methodological support, and the exploration of complex educational problems, while ensuring transparency, data protection, academic integrity, and independent validation of results.I also consider it essential to develop new methodological and technological capabilities, promote AI literacy among educators and researchers, and strengthen international academic collaboration.My objective is not to compete with AI or delegate scientific judgment to it, but to develop a complementary research approach in which technological innovation enhances human creativity, critical thinking, and social responsibility. consensus:
The scientific community should move toward a new research paradigm in which artificial intelligence enhances scientific capabilities without weakening human responsibility, critical thinking, or ethical accountability.

This transformation requires clear international frameworks for AI governance, transparency in AI-assisted research, rigorous validation of scientific findings, protection of research data, and explicit standards for authorship, intellectual property, and academic integrity. Human oversight must remain essential, particularly in peer review, editorial decisions, and research funding.

Universities and research institutions should also invest in AI literacy, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the continuous development of methodological and ethical capabilities among researchers.

Equally important, the scientific community must address inequalities in access to advanced AI technologies, ensuring that researchers from developing countries and underrepresented institutions can participate meaningfully in scientific innovation.

Finally, scientific progress should not be measured solely by the speed or volume of discoveries, but also by their reliability, social relevance, inclusiveness, and contribution to human well-being.

AI should help us produce better science, not simply more science. The ultimate responsibility for scientific decisions and their consequences must remain human.
comment:
I would like to emphasize that the future of AI-driven scientific research should be examined not only in terms of technological capabilities and productivity, but also through the lenses of epistemic diversity, scientific equity, and social responsibility.

From a Latin American educational research perspective, one of the greatest challenges is ensuring that AI does not reinforce existing inequalities between countries, institutions, languages, and research traditions. Scientific knowledge must not become increasingly dependent on a small number of technological corporations or dominant epistemological frameworks.

AI systems should support methodological pluralism, recognize diverse cultural and educational contexts, and expand opportunities for researchers working in historically underrepresented regions.

Furthermore, human oversight should be understood as meaningful scientific and ethical responsibility, rather than merely approving automatically generated results.

I believe the fundamental question is not simply how much independence AI should have in science, but under what conditions, with whose participation, for whose benefit, and with what mechanisms of accountability that independence should be exercised.

The future of science should be technologically advanced, but also democratic, inclusive, ethically responsible, and genuinely committed to human development.

consensus:
The scientific community should move from simply adopting AI tools toward fundamentally rethinking how research is conducted, evaluated, and communicated. AI literacy and responsible human–AI collaboration should become integral to research training, while scientific institutions should establish clear standards for transparency, reproducibility, validation, accountability, and ethical oversight.
I believe AI should be encouraged to perform well-defined research tasks autonomously where appropriate, but human researchers must remain accountable for scientific integrity, critical interpretation, and consequential decisions. Peer review, publication practices, research funding, and academic evaluation systems should also evolve to recognize AI-assisted discoveries while safeguarding scientific quality and trust.
AI should enhance rather than undermine scientific creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the development of future researchers. The scientific community must also address unequal access to AI technologies, potential biases, data privacy, and the risk of overreliance on automated outputs.
Ultimately, the goal should not be to preserve traditional research practices unchanged, but to build a more efficient, inclusive, trustworthy, and human-centered scientific ecosystem in which AI accelerates discovery while researchers retain intellectual leadership and societal responsibility.
comment:

As AI increasingly generates hypotheses, analyses, manuscripts, and potentially original discoveries, we must ensure that scientific quality, reproducibility, clinical relevance, and societal value remain more important than the volume of research outputs.
I am particularly concerned about how AI may reshape the development of early-career researchers. If fundamental scientific tasks become automated, we must ensure that the next generation still develops deep disciplinary knowledge, critical thinking, methodological competence, and independent scientific judgment.
I also believe we need to reconsider how scientific contributions are evaluated. Academic recognition should increasingly emphasize originality, rigorous validation, meaningful impact, and responsible innovation rather than publication quantity.
I hope discussions about AI autonomy will include researchers from diverse disciplines, career stages, and geographical regions. The future of science should not be determined by technological capability alone, but by collective decisions about the kind of scientific community we want to build.

consensus:
Research needs to be done on how much AI is effective in actually doing research and providing accurate data.

The scientific community should first conduct extensive independent research to evaluate how effective AI systems actually are in performing scientific research and producing accurate, reliable, and verifiable data. There should be systematic assessments of AI-generated findings, mathematical proofs, research papers, and conclusions across different disciplines.

AI-generated information should not automatically be considered factual. Researchers must establish proper verification mechanisms, transparency standards, and accountability for AI-assisted research. Particular attention should be given to hallucinations, fabricated references, data inaccuracies, bias, and reproducibility.

The scientific community should encourage AI adoption, but it must not sacrifice scientific integrity or human critical thinking. Domain experts should remain involved in validating findings, reviewing research, and making important scientific decisions.

Before treating AI as an independent scientific researcher, we need evidence-based studies demonstrating its actual capabilities, limitations, and consistency.
comment:
AI is undoubtedly one of the most significant technological developments of our time, but there is a need to distinguish between AI's ability to generate information and its ability to generate genuine, accurate knowledge.

Having worked as an AI trainer for several years, I have observed that AI systems can produce convincing answers that are not necessarily factually correct. This is particularly concerning in scientific research, where inaccurate information can lead to misleading conclusions and potentially affect future research.

I believe independent evaluation, transparency, data accuracy, reproducibility, and human accountability should be central to the future of AI-driven scientific research. We should not measure AI's scientific capabilities merely by the volume of papers, proofs, or answers it generates, but by the quality, originality, accuracy, and reproducibility of its contributions.

AI should empower human intelligence, not replace critical thinking. The scientific community must remain open to innovation while exercising caution and maintaining rigorous standards of evidence.

future_5_TEXT: I work at the intersection of literature, publishing, and independent interdisciplinary research. My long-term strategy is not to compete with artificial intelligence, but to develop methods that allow humans and AI systems to collaborate without surrendering human judgment.I already use AI to explore scientific hypotheses, challenge assumptions, develop conceptual models, and create literary works. However, I believe the greatest challenge is not increasing AI capabilities, but establishing reliable mechanisms for transparency, verification, accountability, and revocability.My strategy is to build workflows in which AI can propose, question, simulate, and even challenge my conclusions, while preserving a clear distinction between established evidence, interpretation, and speculation.As AI becomes increasingly autonomous, I believe the most valuable human contribution will be the ability to formulate meaningful questions, recognize uncertainty, and decide when a process should not proceed.For me, the future is not about replacing human intelligence, but about designing responsible cooperation between different forms of intelligence.
consensus:
The scientific community should move beyond simply adopting AI tools and begin developing institutional frameworks for responsible human–AI collaboration.

AI-generated hypotheses, simulations, and interpretations should remain distinguishable from experimentally validated findings. Reproducibility, independent verification, transparency, and accountability must become central requirements, especially as AI systems gain greater autonomy.

I believe scientific institutions should establish explicit boundaries of authority, mechanisms for continuous auditing, and the ability to revoke AI autonomy when necessary.

Most importantly, science must preserve the legitimacy of uncertainty, disagreement, and inconclusive results. An AI system should never be rewarded merely for producing an answer when the evidence does not justify one.

The objective should not be to accelerate scientific output at any cost, but to increase our capacity to investigate reality without compromising the integrity of the scientific method.
comment:
I would like to offer one additional perspective: as AI becomes more capable, we should pay as much attention to the architecture of its limitations as we do to the expansion of its capabilities.

In my independent research and literary work, I have explored a principle that I consider fundamental: the ability to act does not necessarily imply the authority to act.

An AI system may be technically capable of conducting an investigation, generating conclusions, or making decisions. However, its autonomy should remain conditional upon transparency, accountability, independent verification, and revocability.

I am particularly interested in the idea that a well-designed system must preserve the possibility of correction, interruption, and even deliberate non-completion. These are not necessarily failures; they may be essential safeguards against unjustified certainty.

I have explored these questions in a philosophical essay, *The Architecture That Is Never Built*, which examines why preserving the possibility of not completing a process can be an essential feature of responsible institutional design.

I would be pleased to exchange ideas with researchers interested in these questions.

Thank you for creating this opportunity for reflection.

future_5_TEXT: My long-term strategy is to advance human–AI collaborative intelligence while ensuring that increasing AI autonomy does not diminish human authority, authorship or accountability.Through Third Vision AI, I am developing and testing governance architectures that move beyond AI oversight towards accountable execution, evidence integrity and continuous assurance.My approach is grounded in Third Mind (Human + Human + AI), HAAA (Human with Authority, Authorship & Accountability), and Triple Intelligence (Human Intelligence + Artificial Intelligence = Execution Intelligence).I believe the future of research lies not in replacing human intelligence but in combining human intuition, lived experience, scientific evidence and AI capabilities to discover new knowledge and solve complex problems.My strategy is to develop practical, interdisciplinary systems where AI can operate with increasing independence within defined boundaries, while humans retain meaningful authority over consequential decisions.The central question guiding my work is not simply what AI will become capable of doing, but how we preserve human agency, responsibility and scientific integrity as those capabilities evolve.
consensus:
I believe the scientific community needs to rethink how we work with AI, rather than simply focus on what AI can do.

We have an opportunity to bring together academic knowledge, scientific evidence, professional experience, human intuition and the lived experiences of ordinary people. Each brings something valuable, and I don’t believe one should automatically outweigh the others.

Having worked with people for many years, I’ve seen how lived experience can reveal things that formal research may not yet recognise or fully understand. That doesn’t make scientific evidence less important. It means we should be asking better questions and listening to more perspectives.

I also believe we need to be clear about who makes decisions when AI becomes more capable of working independently. AI can help us research, discover and solve problems but people must retain the authority to question its findings, challenge its reasoning and decide what happens next.

This is why my work focuses on human authority, authorship and accountability, alongside collaborative intelligence.

For me, the future of research isn’t about choosing between human intelligence and artificial intelligence. It’s about learning how to bring them together responsibly, while making room for knowledge and experiences that may have been overlooked.

Scientific evidence doesn’t eliminate lived experience, and neither does artificial intelligence replace human intelligence.
comment:
I believe AI can become a valuable collaborative thinking partner in the scientific community.

As humans, we bring so many ideas, concepts, experiences, answered and unanswered questions to the table. AI shouldn’t be doing the thinking for us. It should help us explore and structure our thoughts, find relevant research, challenge our assumptions and introduce information or perspectives that might spark new ideas.

Sometimes we don’t even know what questions to ask until we start exploring an idea together. That’s where I see the real value of human–AI collaboration.

For me, AI is not a replacement for human curiosity, intuition, lived experience or scientific knowledge. It’s an opportunity to bring these together and expand what we can discover.

I call this my Third Mind approach: Human + Human + AI. We bring our intelligence, experiences and questions, and AI helps us explore possibilities we may not have considered.

The human remains the thinker, the author and the person accountable for what comes next.

consensus:
I think the first step is simply accepting that AI is here to stay. Resisting it or pretending it’s a passing trend won’t help the scientific community. Our energy is better spent learning to use it well. For me, that means treating it as an opportunity to train our models ethically and precisely, and doing it continuously, in a cycle that doesn’t stop. A model is only as good as the guidance and checking we give it, so training it isn’t a one-time job.

The bigger shift is in how we prepare new researchers. They need to learn to work with AI as team leaders, not as passive receivers of whatever it produces. That means understanding how these systems actually operate, what they do well, where they fail, and why. It also means getting hands-on experience directing them, questioning their outputs, and refining them over time.

If we get this right, AI won’t replace researchers’ judgement. It will speed up the process of sharing insights and ideas with the world.

consensus:
The scientific community should embrace AI as a transformative research tool while establishing clear standards for transparency, reproducibility, independent validation, and human accountability.
AI-generated hypotheses, analyses, and findings should be critically evaluated rather than accepted solely on the basis of computational performance. Scientific journals, universities, and funding agencies should develop consistent policies for responsible AI use, disclosure, and research integrity.
Research training should also evolve to combine AI literacy with critical thinking, disciplinary expertise, and ethical judgment. Above all, AI should accelerate scientific discovery without compromising the reliability, independence, and public trustworthiness of science.
comment:
One important distinction deserves greater attention: the difference between AI's ability to generate scientific results and its ability to establish their scientific validity.
In environmental and ecological research, a statistically convincing result does not necessarily represent ecological truth. Field observations, biological mechanisms, spatial and temporal variability, and independent validation remain essential.
As AI becomes more autonomous, the scientific community must ensure that faster discovery does not come at the expense of reliability, reproducibility, or accountability.
The future of science should not be defined simply by how independently AI can conduct research, but by how effectively humans and AI can work together to produce trustworthy knowledge. Human researchers must remain responsible for the scientific claims they endorse.

future_5_TEXT: I intend to integrate AI more systematically into my long-term research practice, treating it as an advanced research-support tool rather than an autonomous authority or a substitute for human scientific judgment.I see significant potential in using AI for literature discovery, source analysis, information synthesis, identifying patterns and inconsistencies, exploring hypotheses, and supporting the development of research methodologies. These capabilities may allow independent researchers and small research institutions to undertake more ambitious interdisciplinary projects.At the same time, I believe that long-term research strategy must prioritize methodological transparency, source verification, reproducibility, and clear human accountability. AI-generated outputs should be critically evaluated, particularly when they concern factual claims, legal interpretation, scientific evidence, or conclusions that may influence public understanding.I also intend to study how AI changes the nature of research itself, including questions of authorship, intellectual contribution, epistemic responsibility, and the relationship between human researchers and increasingly capable AI systems.Rather than competing with AI or relying on it uncritically, my strategy is to develop the skills and methodologies necessary to use it effectively while preserving independent judgment and responsibility for the research process and its published conclusions.
consensus:
The scientific community should adapt proactively, but carefully and critically. Rather than treating AI as either a threat to scientific integrity or a universal solution, it should develop clear methodological standards for its responsible use.

First, scientific institutions should establish transparent guidelines for disclosing AI involvement in research, including literature reviews, data analysis, writing, interpretation, and other research activities. Such guidelines should distinguish between different levels and types of AI assistance rather than treating all uses as equivalent.

Second, the community should strengthen standards for source verification, reproducibility, data integrity, and human accountability. AI-generated content should not be accepted as evidence in itself, and researchers must remain responsible for the accuracy and validity of their findings.

Third, scientific education should evolve. Researchers and students need to understand not only how to use AI tools, but also their technical limitations, biases, failure modes, and epistemological implications.

Finally, the scientific community should reconsider existing assumptions about authorship, intellectual contribution, peer review, and access to research capabilities. AI may significantly reduce some barriers to conducting interdisciplinary research, potentially allowing independent researchers and smaller institutions to contribute more effectively to scientific discourse.

I believe the goal should not be to preserve existing research practices unchanged, nor to delegate scientific judgment to AI. It should be to develop a research environment in which human expertise and AI capabilities complement each other, while scientific standards, transparency, and intellectual responsibility remain central.
comment:
One additional point I would like to emphasize is that AI should not be viewed solely as a tool for increasing research efficiency. Its development raises more fundamental questions about the nature of scientific work, intellectual contribution, knowledge production, and research independence.

In particular, I believe that AI creates new opportunities for independent researchers and smaller research institutions. Access to advanced analytical capabilities may reduce some of the traditional barriers associated with interdisciplinary research, literature analysis, and the development of complex research projects.

However, this opportunity also creates a need for more precise methodological standards. It is important to distinguish between using AI as an instrument, using it as an analytical collaborator, and delegating intellectual tasks to it without adequate human verification.

An especially important area requiring further research is the problem of AI hallucinations and errors. These should be examined not only as isolated technical failures, but also in comparison with traditional errors in scientific work. For example, AI systems may generate nonexistent bibliographic references, misattribute publications, distort the findings of existing sources, or produce inaccurate statements within otherwise coherent texts. Similar problems can also occur in human research, including incorrect citations, misinterpretation of literature, factual inaccuracies, and methodological oversights.

It is therefore important to investigate whether AI introduces fundamentally new categories of research errors, how its errors differ from traditional human errors, and whether existing scientific verification procedures are sufficient to identify them. This should also include linguistic and grammatical accuracy, since AI-generated texts may appear fluent and professionally written while containing subtle semantic, terminological, grammatical, or stylistic inconsistencies.

I would also encourage the scientific community to study these changes empirically rather than relying exclusively on assumptions about the future of AI. We need to understand how researchers actually use these systems, how they affect the quality and originality of research, and how responsibility should be distributed throughout the research process.

Ultimately, AI development should encourage us to reconsider what makes research reliable, independent, and scientifically valuable.

consensus:
Artificial intelligence is no longer just one tool among many in the laboratory. In a few years it has gone from a specialised method to something that runs through the whole research process. Researchers now use it to search the literature, form hypotheses, analyse data, write code, draft manuscripts and even review them. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded partly for AI-based protein structure prediction, showed that these systems can now contribute to discoveries in their own right. So the real question for the scientific community is how to adapt, not whether to.

Adaptation is needed because AI changes things faster than the norms that hold science together. Reproducibility, transparency, accountability and peer review all assume that a human researcher can explain and defend every step of the work. A model that suggests an analysis, writes the statistics code or summarises fifty papers in a few seconds can be very helpful. It can also be wrong with complete confidence, invent references, or carry over the biases in its training data. If no one checks, these errors spread quietly through the literature.

I think the community should respond in four ways.

First, disclosure should be specific and routine. A vague statement that “AI tools were used” tells a reader almost nothing. Methods sections should say which tool was used, for which step and how its output was checked, just as they already report software versions and statistical tests. AI use is not a confession. It is part of the methodology.

Second, responsibility must stay with people. An AI system cannot be an author, because it cannot take responsibility for errors, answer reviewers or retract a claim. Every number, citation and conclusion in a paper is the responsibility of the people who signed it. That includes verifying every reference and rerunning every AI-generated analysis.

Third, training needs to change. Students learn statistics so they can tell when a result does not make sense, not just so they can calculate it. The same applies to AI. The next generation of researchers will need to know what these systems do well, where they fail and how to check what they produce. Without that judgement, AI makes researchers faster at making mistakes rather than more productive.

Fourth, institutions must protect the integrity of publishing. Generative tools make it cheap to produce fabricated papers, manipulated images and low-quality submissions in large numbers. Journals, funders and ethics committees will need better screening, stronger requirements for sharing data and code, and more support for the reviewers who carry the extra workload.

Adaptation does not mean surrender. Some of the most valuable parts of science are slow on purpose: designing an experiment carefully, doubting your own results, and having findings checked independently by others. AI should speed up the routine work so that researchers have more time for these parts, not less. If the community sets clear rules now, AI could make science broader, more open and more reproducible. If it does not, AI will set the rules by default, and they are unlikely to be the ones science needs.

future_5_TEXT: In light of recent developments in Artificial Intelligence, I intend to develop long-term strategies focused on continuously updating my knowledge and research skills, strengthening my expertise in AI, cybersecurity, digital forensics, and public safety.I plan to integrate advanced AI tools into my research activities while maintaining human oversight, scientific integrity, and ethical responsibility. I also aim to explore emerging areas such as autonomous AI systems, AI-driven cybercrime, deepfakes, digital evidence manipulation, and the impact of AI on institutional security.Furthermore, I intend to strengthen international research collaborations, publish scientific papers, participate in interdisciplinary projects, and contribute to the development of policies and frameworks for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence, particularly in Angola and across Africa.My long-term goal is to establish myself as an active contributor to AI research and innovation, ensuring that technological progress supports human development, public safety, and scientific advancement rather than replacing human judgment and accountability.
consensus:
The scientific community should adapt to recent developments in Artificial Intelligence by embracing technological innovation while maintaining human responsibility, scientific integrity, and ethical standards.

Universities, research institutions, and scientific journals should establish clear guidelines for the responsible use of AI in research, including transparency about AI-assisted work, data protection, proper attribution, and the verification of AI-generated information.

Researchers should also receive continuous training to develop AI literacy, critical thinking, and the ability to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated results. Rather than viewing AI as a replacement for researchers, it should be treated as a tool that enhances human capabilities, accelerates scientific discovery, and supports data analysis.

Furthermore, the scientific community should strengthen interdisciplinary and international collaboration to address emerging challenges such as misinformation, deepfakes, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity threats, and the manipulation of scientific evidence.

In my view, the future of scientific research should be based on a model of AI-assisted research with human supervision, in which AI can perform increasingly complex tasks, but humans retain responsibility for scientific decisions, ethical considerations, and the validation of research findings. This adaptation is particularly important for developing countries, including Angola, to ensure that they are not left behind in the global transformation of scientific research.
comment:
I believe that Artificial Intelligence represents one of the most significant transformations in the history of scientific research. However, its development should not be measured solely by technological progress, but also by its contribution to humanity, knowledge, public safety, and social development.

One of my main concerns is the growing possibility of AI systems generating scientific information, analysing evidence, and making increasingly autonomous decisions without sufficient human supervision. This raises important questions about accountability, transparency, scientific credibility, and the future role of human researchers.

I believe that the scientific community should work towards establishing a framework of Human-Supervised Artificial Intelligence, ensuring that AI systems can support and accelerate research while humans retain ultimate responsibility for critical decisions and ethical standards.

I would also like to emphasise the importance of including researchers from developing countries, particularly Angola and other African nations, in international discussions about the future of AI. These countries should not be merely consumers of technologies developed elsewhere; they should also participate in scientific innovation, research, policy development, and global AI governance.

Ultimately, I believe that the future of science should not be a competition between humans and Artificial Intelligence, but a responsible partnership in which technological intelligence serves humanity, rather than humanity becoming dependent on autonomous technological systems.

Gelson Jacinto
Independent AI Researcher
Luanda, Angola

1. Employment opportunities for younger generations: AI poses a significant and potentially disruptive threat to young people entering society and the workforce.

Promote and monitor responsible use. If scientific journals charge subscription fees, they should remunerate the anonymous peer reviewers who evaluate scientific articles. Public institutions, including universities and government bodies, should reduce or eliminate payments to foreign academic publishers that charge open-access publication fees without redistributing this revenue to reviewers or the wider scientific community.

Reduce or eliminate automatically AI-generated texts. It is often quite obvious when a text has been written by AI. Such texts tend to exhibit distinctive stylistic tics, recurring expressions, circumlocutions, excessive use of adverbs, and grammatical patterns that unmistakably reveal their AI-generated nature. They are unpleasant to read and significantly undermine the depth of thought, the ability to connect what is being read with prior knowledge, and the development of critical thinking.

Address the biases inherent in AI-assisted literature searches. AI systems are trained on texts published by major multinational academic publishers, many of which operate behind paywalls. This creates a knowledge bias that privileges publications from the Anglo-Saxon academic world. Scientific research produced within Mediterranean cultural traditions—including Greek, Italian, French, Spanish, and Portuguese traditions—as well as across the broader Hispanic American cultural sphere, loses visibility and representation in AI-assisted bibliographic searches. It is therefore essential to conduct targeted literature searches and promote the use of academic databases that specifically represent scientific production from non-Anglo-Saxon cultural and academic traditions.

consensus:
This is a very difficult question. Up until now, the scientific community could be considered an elite within the system. However, with the use of AI, it seems many more people could become part of that elite. Consequently, the nature of research is shifting, as there is no longer any control over what gets published.
I am aware that the production of scientific articles has grown enormously in recent years. The speed at which information, both high- and low-quality, is being generated is overwhelming. I am not entirely sure what the best approach is to prevent scientific journals from becoming a newspapers, but I see two possible paths.

The first approach would be to entrust peer review to individuals with solid scientific experience and training in using AI. I believe this foundational experience is essential, as domain specific knowledge is required to validate what AI produces. However, individuals with this profile tend to be older and may adapt more slowly to incorporating these tools into their evaluation processes. This could create a knowledge backlog that is not published at the same rate it is produced. Furthermore, the pool of editors and reviewers could effectively become an exclusive elite of experts.

The second approach would be to abandon the current model of dissemination through scientific journals, with established research groups instead disseminating their own findings, much like an open marketplace. However, because, as in many other industries, scientific publishing involves a large deal of money, I consider this scenario less likely.
comment: I have a few comments on this. I believe AI contributes significantly to the drafting, structuring, and data processing involved in scientific articles; however, the information used to generate this content is largely provided by humans—for instance, through laboratory experiments involving food, human subjects, and so on. Therefore, I do not believe AI will ever be capable of conducting research independently to the point of generating new knowledge, as experiments in the field are inherently a human endeavor. As for whether this affects the profession of scientific research—yes, I believe it does, though not in terms of its viability. The profession will continue to exist, but it may no longer be an "elite" field; its status might shift, either because there will be more researchers across a wider range of areas, or perhaps because two distinct types of researchers will emerge. Finally, regarding whether this has led me to reconsider my own career path: no. I remain committed to conducting ethical research and publishing in journals that employ transparent review processes and are well-regarded by the scientific community. I want to publish work that I have personally read and evaluated—work that I believe offers a genuine contribution and is backed by experts in the field who were trained before the advent of AI.

future_5_TEXT: My long-term strategy is to use AI to support my work while continuing to develop the judgement on which that work depends. As a researcher, professor and consultant, I want to devote more time to questions worth pursuing, to listening closely, and to making decisions I can explain and take responsibility for.In research, AI can help me organise materials, test the structure of an argument or refine a translation. The interpretation still has to be grounded in sources I have examined, in dialogue with the people and phenomena I study, and in a clear account of how I reached my conclusions. In my lessons, this means asking how what we hear relates to history, philosophy, politics or social life, and what evidence allows us to draw those connections. For example, as an ethnomusicologist and a musicologist, it is important to understand that a musical practice may take on a different meaning when we consider who performs it, who listens to it and the institutions that give it a public place.The same principle applies to consultancy: a tool can help compare scenarios, but deciding what counts as prosperity for a community requires listening to the people who live there and recognising what the available indicators leave out. In composition, I can decide where a tool serves the work while retaining responsibility for the musical choices through which it acquires its character.Over time, I intend to keep learning how these systems work and to assess them against a practical question: does using AI give me more time and attention for the work that matters, or does it gradually take over a practice through which I learn to think, listen and create? Using AI deliberately and critically is central to how I want to work.
consensus:
I believe the scientific community should adapt by making the use of AI open to the same critical scrutiny as any other part of the research process. 

When AI plays a substantive role in an analysis, researchers should explain how it was used, how they checked its outputs and how those outputs informed their conclusions. 

In ethnomusicology, musicology, neuromusicology, for example, AI might help identify patterns across a collection of recordings. But, interpreting those patterns requires listening closely, understanding the circumstances in which the recordings were made and considering how musicians themselves understand their practices.

For me, the most important adaptation is educational. We should teach researchers to question the assumptions behind AI-generated outputs and to make connections across disciplines with care. An AI system might suggest a link between a musical practice and a political movement. Despite this, the researcher still has to ask and think criticaly of what kind of link is being proposed, which sources could substantiate it and how the explanation changes when approached from historical, sociological or musical perspectives.

Nevertheless, researchers remain responsible for the conclusions they draw.
