consensus:
Para que la comunidad científica no solo sobreviva, sino que lidere en la era de la inteligencia artificial, la adaptación es indispensable. No se trata de incorporar software de forma pasiva, sino de reestructurar los pilares éticos, metodológicos y educativos de la ciencia.
La comunidad científica debería adaptarse enfocándose en cuatro ejes críticos:

1. Redefinición de la Integridad Científica y el Plagio

• Transparencia algorítmica: Los investigadores deben reportar con total claridad qué herramientas de IA utilizaron, con qué prompts y en qué fases del estudio (recolección, análisis o redacción).
• Políticas editoriales claras: Las revistas científicas deben estandarizar el uso de IA, prohibiendo de forma tajante que los modelos de lenguaje figuren como "coautores", ya que la IA carece de responsabilidad legal y ética sobre lo publicado.

2. Reformulación de los Criterios de Evaluación

• Crisis de la revisión por pares (Peer Review): La IA puede generar manuscritos falsos o datos sintéticos increíblemente realistas. La comunidad debe transicionar hacia sistemas de evaluación que prioricen la replicabilidad real y la auditoría de datos crudos sobre la simple lectura del texto.
• Nuevas métricas de impacto: El mérito académico ya no puede medirse solo por la cantidad de papers publicados, dado que la IA acelera la redacción de manuscritos a niveles industriales. Se debe premiar la originalidad y el impacto real en el mundo físico.

3. Democratización del Acceso y Brecha Tecnológica

• Evitar el oligopolio tecnológico: Actualmente, los modelos de IA más potentes están en manos de un puñado de corporaciones privadas. La comunidad científica debe exigir y financiar infraestructuras públicas de IA de código abierto para que los laboratorios de países en desarrollo puedan competir en igualdad de condiciones.
• Inclusión digital: Diseñar programas globales para que la brecha de recursos entre instituciones no se amplíe críticamente debido al costo de cómputo.

4. Transformación de la Educación Científica

• Alfabetización en IA desde el pregrado: La formación de los nuevos científicos debe incluir obligatoriamente estadística avanzada, programación básica y ética computacional.
• Foco en habilidades humanas irreemplazables: La educación debe dejar de premiar la memorización o la redacción mecánica, y volcarse al desarrollo de la intuición científica, el diseño experimental creativo, la empatía y la resolución de problemas complejos en el terreno.

future_5_TEXT: As I mentioned earlier, I believe that, in the social sciences, artificial intelligence is unlikely to make substantive theoretical contributions autonomously. This is primarily due to the limitations of its interpretive capacity to formulate original research questions, develop sociological explanations, and understand phenomena shaped by emotions, values, moralities, power relations, and historically situated symbolic constructions. Although AI can identify patterns, establish associations, and reproduce theoretical arguments, these capabilities do not necessarily amount to an understanding of human experiences and the social conditions that give meaning to such phenomena.For this reason, I do not consider AI a direct threat to the practice of sociology. However, I recognise its potential to transform research procedures, expand analytical possibilities, and reshape the conditions under which knowledge is produced. In this sense, my long-term strategy is to critically engage with these developments and incorporate tools that contribute to scientific research, without delegating to them the theoretical, methodological, and interpretive decisions that are fundamental to the researcher's work. I consider this approach particularly important in countries such as Brazil, where inequalities in access to technology and the reluctance of some sectors of the academic community to adopt new tools may deepen existing asymmetries in scientific knowledge production.
consensus:
As in other sectors that have already adopted artificial intelligence, I believe the scientific community should explore its potential to accelerate the production, evaluation, and dissemination of knowledge. In particular, I believe that some of AI's most important contributions could lie in transforming academic publishing and expanding public access to scientific knowledge.

In Brazil, as I believe is also the case in other countries, I would highlight two problems in the academic publishing process. The first is the slow pace of peer review, which can delay the publication of articles for years, partly due to difficulties in finding available reviewers. Peer review relies on highly specialised work that is generally unpaid and carried out by researchers who are already overwhelmed by other responsibilities. In this context, AI tools could help identify reviewers with appropriate expertise, conduct preliminary assessments of methodological aspects, and detect inconsistencies in manuscripts, reducing some of the operational workload and allowing human reviewers to focus their efforts on evaluating the scientific contributions of studies.

The second problem concerns editorial bias and hierarchies of academic prestige. Senior researchers or those affiliated with prestigious institutions may enjoy more favourable publication opportunities, even when their work does not offer particularly innovative contributions, while early-career researchers face greater difficulties in gaining recognition. AI could help address these inequalities through anonymous preliminary assessment systems based on explicit criteria of quality, originality, and methodological consistency. It could also assist in monitoring editorial decisions, making it possible to identify patterns of preferential treatment associated with authors' reputations or institutional affiliations.

A third contribution, which I consider particularly relevant, would be the use of AI to expand the dissemination of scientific knowledge beyond academic circles. Currently, a substantial proportion of the knowledge produced in universities remains confined to specialised publications, written in language that is difficult for non-specialists to understand and intended for a relatively small audience. AI tools could help transform research findings into accessible science communication materials, such as news articles, videos, podcasts, infographics, and educational content adapted to different audiences and educational backgrounds. They could also facilitate the translation of publications into other languages and the creation of resources that allow people to explore research findings and understand their implications for problems affecting their everyday lives. In countries marked by deep educational and social inequalities, such as Brazil, I believe this possibility is especially important. Of course, making scientific language more accessible must not compromise scientific rigour, and it is essential to preserve the limitations, uncertainties, and context of the findings being communicated. Researchers' oversight would remain fundamental.

Naturally, the adoption of these technologies would require mechanisms for transparency, human oversight, and continuous evaluation, since AI systems themselves can reproduce biases already present in scientific knowledge production. Nor do I believe that these tools can replace the need to value and recognise the work of peer reviewers or to reform institutional practices that perpetuate academic inequalities.

consensus:
The scientific community should embrace AI as an opportunity to democratize research, enabling more researchers to address complex questions with fewer resources.

However, greater scientific productivity does not necessarily mean greater scientific progress. Widespread reliance on similar AI models and knowledge sources may lead to epistemic homogenization, reducing the diversity of hypotheses, methodologies and perspectives.

I believe the scientific community should develop new standards for transparency, reproducibility, independent validation and effective human oversight. Researchers should diversify their sources of evidence, including through approaches such as RAG, and critically evaluate AI-generated conclusions.

Scientific institutions must also strengthen their governance capabilities, ensuring that responsibility, intellectual independence and scientific integrity remain central as AI systems become increasingly autonomous.

The goal should not simply be to produce more research, but to produce better, more diverse and trustworthy knowledge.
comment:
Thank you for conducting this timely and relevant study.

I would like to highlight a potential paradox: AI is making scientific research more accessible, enabling individuals and small research teams to undertake projects that would previously have required substantially greater resources. My own research experience reflects this opportunity.

However, I believe we should also investigate whether widespread reliance on the same foundation models may unintentionally lead to a convergence of research questions, methodologies and conclusions, potentially reducing epistemic diversity.

This is not an established conclusion, but a hypothesis worth investigating. Diversified knowledge sources, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), independent validation and effective human oversight may help mitigate this risk.

In my view, the central challenge is not only how autonomous AI can become in scientific research, but whether researchers and scientific institutions can develop the governance capabilities needed to preserve intellectual independence, scientific integrity and accountability.

I would be very interested in learning about the findings of this study and any future research addressing these questions.

future_5_TEXT: Long-term Strategy for AI in Research and DevelopmentTo maintain relevance and boost productivity in R&D projects, the long-term strategy involves integrating artificial intelligence as a methodological co-pilot. This allows for the delegation of repetitive operational tasks, enabling human effort to be focused on experimental design, critical thinking, and scientific validation.The workflow is structured around five key areas:• Literature research and synthesis: Utilizing specialized semantic search engines to track the state of the art, extract methodologies into comparative tables, and consistently verify primary sources to avoid biases or fabricated citations.• Scientific writing: Providing raw notes to AI models to structure initial drafts, refine academic style, and translate technical concepts—while maintaining absolute human oversight over the final conclusions.• Protocol generation: Employing AI as a preliminary auditor to standardize procedures according to international guidelines, create checklists, and identify potential confounding variables or reproducibility issues before experimentation begins.• Linking hypotheses to statistics: Using AI assistants to map variables, justify the selection of statistical models based on data distribution, and validate sample power assumptions as early as the design phase.• Mathematical clarity and rigor: Avoiding direct calculation within text-based AI models; instead, using AI to generate auditable scripts (in Python or R), break down formulas step-by-step, and test models using synthetic data before analyzing actual results.Key to sustainability: Future success will depend on standardizing these instructions into reusable workflows, protecting the intellectual property of unpublished data, and rigorously auditing every output generated by the AI.
consensus:
Human oversight and traceability in the laboratory.
• Mandatory validation by the researcher. Any result, code, statistical analysis, or text generated using artificial intelligence tools must undergo an audit documented by the lead researcher or operational staff. This record verifies the absence of biases, "hallucinations," or methodological errors prior to publication or application.
• Transparent disclosure of use. Scientific journals and ethics committees require a detailed account of which model was used, at what stage of the study it was employed, and the specific prompts or instructions provided. As noted by meta-science researchers such as Balázs Aczél, standardizing the attribution of tasks between humans and automated systems helps safeguard reproducibility.
• Legal and ethical responsibility. AI systems cannot be listed as authors, nor can they assume legal liability. Authorship and ethical accountability rest exclusively with the human researchers who sign off on and oversee the work.
Legal harmonization and regulatory standards (ICH and academia)
• Integration into ICH guidelines. In clinical and pharmaceutical research, the guidelines of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH)—such as Good Clinical Practice (ICH E6)—must incorporate specific protocols regarding the use of algorithms in trial design, data monitoring, and pharmacovigilance. This ensures that data submitted to regulatory agencies maintain traceability and uphold patient safety.
• National laws and data governance. Each country requires binding legislation to regulate the training of models using sensitive scientific data, protect the privacy of study participants, and establish penalties for the fabrication or manipulation of results through automated tools.
• Institutional regulations in academia. Universities and research centers require clear internal policies that define the acceptable limits of automation in theses, peer reviews, and grant applications, ensuring that the speed of output does not come at the expense of methodological rigor. Adaptation to Emerging Technologies

• Flexible and forward-looking regulatory frameworks. Laws and academic guidelines should be drafted based on principles of technological neutrality and risk assessment, rather than being limited to current tools. This ensures that regulations remain relevant as more advanced autonomous systems, quantum computing, or next-generation multimodal models emerge.
• Continuous training in algorithmic auditing. The education of new scientists and operators must include the skills to audit automated systems, identify reasoning flaws in complex models, and implement rigorous quality controls at every stage of the scientific method.

consensus: Adapting to recent developments in artificial intelligence requires the scientific community to evolve structurally, ethically, and epistemically. Rather than simply using AI to speed up existing routines, academia and scientific institutions must update fundamental standards governing how research is conducted, evaluated, and shared.   The key areas where the scientific community needs to adapt encompass four main dimensions:1. Verification and Epistemic Rigor (From "Speed" to "Validation")Mitigating the "Noise Horizon": As generative AI reduces the cost of producing plausible text, code, and hypotheses to near zero, the scientific community faces a flood of low-friction research and potential hallucinations. Focus must shift from generating volume to rigorous verification and auditing.   Benchmark & Data Integrity: Autonomous data processing demands new validation protocols for datasets. Scientific fields require strict data-provenance tracking (e.g., cryptographic hashing, explicit data lineage) to prevent synthetic or machine-contaminated data from corrupting foundational models.Reproducibility of AI Workflows: Traditional reproducibility meant sharing code and data. With non-deterministic AI models and automated agents, institutions must establish standards for documenting exact prompt histories, temperature settings, seed numbers, model versions, and environmental parameters.
comment:
To synthesize the conversation, the integration of AI into scientific research comes down to a fundamental trade-off: scale vs. signal.

While AI dramatically lowers the friction of gathering data, generating hypotheses, and drafting manuscripts, it simultaneously increases the risk of low-quality noise and unverified claims flooding the literature. The most successful approach for individual researchers and institutions alike will not be passive resistance or unchecked adoption, but intentional orchestration.

A few final core principles to keep in mind:

Human Accountability Remains Immutable: Tools can assist with analysis and execution, but responsibility for validity, safety, and ethical boundaries rests solely with human authors and institutional oversight.

Valuing the Unexpected: Machine learning models extrapolate patterns from existing data; they excel at optimization within known parameters. Genuine scientific breakthroughs often depend on human intuition, serendipity, and identifying anomalies that models dismiss as outliers.

Preserving Scientific Diversity: As standardized AI platforms become common baseline tools, maintaining diverse research perspectives, interdisciplinary paradigms, and qualitative approaches will be essential to prevent field-wide cognitive lock-in.

Addressing these shifts proactively allows scientists to leverage AI as a powerful force multiplier for discovery while maintaining the epistemic rigor that gives science its authority.

consensus: I think that we cannot make sweeping generalisations about AI. Its positive or negative impact varies enormously depending on the field of research in question, and I would also say on the country in which one works. In some fields, the risk of AI leading to job losses is very real. In my own field, however, employment opportunities are already limited, and AI could actually help us manage workloads that can sometimes be overwhelming, reducing the time spent on the less productive aspects of academic research. I think that researchers should be encouraged to explore these possibilities, develop the skills needed to use AI critically, and identify where it can genuinely improve their work without compromising academic rigour or intellectual independence. At the same time, clear guidelines and some degree of regulation should probably be established by universities, research institutions, funding bodies, and academic publishers to ensure the responsible and transparent use of AI in academic research.

The scientific community should actively adopt AI while maintaining human responsibility for scientific judgment.

AI can greatly accelerate research, but it is biased toward existing knowledge and established theories. This can be especially problematic when exploring genuinely new scientific ideas.

Researchers should independently verify AI-generated results, preserve reproducible evidence, and report both positive and negative findings without allowing unsuccessful experiments to prematurely end further exploration.

comment:
I believe an important distinction is being overlooked in discussions about AI-driven science: the ability to solve research problems is not the same as the ability to identify which problems are worth pursuing.

In my own research, AI has proven extremely powerful for mathematical reasoning, computational experiments, and scientific writing. However, I have repeatedly observed biases toward established knowledge, premature conclusions, and difficulties maintaining a coherent research direction without human intervention.

Scientific breakthroughs often require questioning the assumptions underlying existing theories. AI systems should be evaluated not only by the problems they solve, but also by their ability to recognize their own limitations, preserve alternative hypotheses, and respond appropriately to contradictory evidence.

The future of science should not be measured solely by how independently AI can operate, but by how effectively humans and AI can collaborate to discover genuinely new knowledge.

Additionally, I would like to point out that Gmail flagged the survey link in your invitation email as potentially dangerous, warning that the website had previously hosted phishing content.

Although I was eventually able to access the survey, this security warning could discourage other researchers from participating.

I recommend investigating the issue with Google and Qualtrics and considering an alternative distribution method to ensure that legitimate research invitations are not blocked or mistaken for phishing attempts.

I think scientists need strict rules and cultural mores around how AI tools should be used in the practice of science. I think disseminating AI-generated papers or outsourcing paper review to AI is insane and should be entirely prohibited. 

The AI-generated proofs in math were released as a publicity stunt to try to claw out an IPO, not for the advancement of human knowledge. I do not believe they can be trusted as academic work. Period. If some or all of the work contained is true, let it be explored, tested, verified, and re-written by subject experts who can give the proofs meaning in the context of the field of mathematics.
comment:
Is the aim of science to advance technological capacities 

Or is it to use technology to advance human capacities for understanding the natural world ?

If it is the latter, I think it is obvious that overreliance on AI tools poses many near term and long term threats to human understanding, to say nothing of its social impacts. If it is the former, I think overreliance on AI tools trades near term benefit for long term deficits, building a very steep "tech debt."

In short, I believe it is a tool with great promise but also existential danger (not like terminator, but that it will lead us astray, make us stupid, and expose us to new forms of exploitation).

As a librarian, I believe the scientific community should adapt to AI developments by integrating AI into research, information management, and scholarly communication while maintaining academic integrity and critical thinking.

Librarians should take a more active role in this transformation by:
1. Promoting AI literacy: Helping researchers and students understand how to use AI tools effectively and responsibly.
2. Improving research support: Using AI to support literature searches, systematic reviews, bibliometric analysis, and scientific information discovery.
3. Ensuring information reliability: Teaching users to verify AI-generated information, check original references, and recognize misinformation and bias.
4. Supporting research integrity: Educating researchers about transparency, proper AI-use disclosure, copyright, and research ethics.
5. Developing library services: Integrating AI into digital library services, metadata management, information retrieval, and research consultation.

The scientific community should adapt, but it should treat AI as a research tool whose outputs require scrutiny, not as an authority. AI can help researchers search literature, analyse large datasets, generate code, and improve access to scientific work. It can also produce fabricated references, obscure errors in data or code, and reproduce biases in its training material.

Researchers should disclose when and how they use AI, verify generated claims and references, and retain responsibility for the methods and conclusions they publish. Journals and universities should set clear rules for disclosure, data privacy, authorship, and the use of AI in peer review. Training should help researchers assess AI outputs, not merely operate the tools.

The result is that scholars now publish in very small niches and only on a very small and specific topic, they choose the topics and theories that are more realistically interesting for top journals, and split results in as many papers as possible instead of writing one paper dense of interesting results. We publish a lot of pages, with very little value. And this was the publish or perish culture before AI. With AI, this process becomes increasingly faster. Instead of focusing on value, on discovering something new, with the risk of not publishing anything at all if the research doesn't go as intended, AI makes it feasible to write faster, and publish even more. But is the contribution to knowledge and society increasing as fast? What's left of the creativity of being a researcher, of writing a section of a paper not as fast as possible, but slowly, and giving the text the exact meaning that we intend, not the one that the AI decided for us? سؤال ممتاز وجوهري! يُظهر اهتمامك الحقيقي بكيفية تفاعل المجتمع العلمي مع التطورات السريعة في الذكاء الاصطناعي.

بشكل عام، يجب على المجتمع العلمي أن يتبنى نهجًا تكيفيًا يركز على التعاون والمسؤولية الأخلاقية، بدلاً من مجرد تبني الأدوات الجديدة أو مقاومتها. إليك بعض الجوانب الرئيسية التي يمكن أن تتكيف معها:

تعزيز الشفافية وقابلية التفسير (Transparency & Explainability): يجب أن تصبح نماذج الذكاء الاصطناعي "صناديق زجاجية" وليست "صناديق سوداء". العلماء بحاجة إلى فهم كيف تصل هذه النماذج إلى استنتاجاتها، خاصة في مجالات حساسة مثل الطب أو الفيزياء. هذا يعني تطوير معايير جديدة لتوثيق البيانات والخوارزميات المستخدمة.

إعادة صياغة منهجية البحث: لم يعد دور الباحث يقتصر فقط على جمع البيانات وتحليلها يدويًا؛ بل أصبح جزءًا كبيرًا من العمل هو صياغة الأسئلة الصحيحة وتوجيه الذكاء الاصطناعي للبحث عن إجابات محتملة. يمكن استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي لمحاكاة تجارب معقدة أو تحليل مجموعات بيانات ضخمة بسرعة هائلة، مما يسرع الاكتشافات العلمية بشكل غير مسبوق.

Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping how scientific findings are communicated, yet its actual impact on experimental discovery remains deeply uneven. By lowering linguistic barriers, generative AI has leveled the playing field for non-native English speakers, allowing researchers worldwide to articulate complex hypotheses with equal fluency. Beneath this surface-level equity, however, a stark disparity in research depth is emerging. Restricted access to advanced computing infrastructure and frontier models in certain regions threatens to sideline capable scientists, creating a widening global compute divide.

In microbiology, the boundary between AI’s utility and its limitations is particularly sharp. Currently, AI excels in the "dry-lab" arena—accelerating literature synthesis, integrating multi-omics datasets, and predicting putative metabolic pathways. Yet when transitioning to the "wet lab," its direct contribution approaches zero. Microbiology is fundamentally governed by biological unpredictability and physical constraints. Culturing fastidious pathogens, troubleshooting genetic manipulation efficiencies, and validating virulence phenotypes in in vivo infection models require empirical, hands-on iteration at the bench that no algorithm can simulate away.

Compounding this limitation is a growing crisis of data integrity. The biomedical literature is increasingly contaminated by irreproducible findings and fabricated data from paper mills. Because AI models learn indiscriminately from existing publications, this "data poisoning" risks generating plausible-sounding yet biologically flawed hypotheses. Without rigorous experimental verification, over-reliance on AI threatens to amplify misinformation rather than accelerate truth.

AI is undeniably a powerful co-pilot for data triage and scholarly communication, but it is far from ready to take the helm of scientific discovery. In microbiology, genuine breakthroughs are still forged through meticulous benchwork—and no language model can replace the reality of the Petri dish.

future_5_TEXT: We must become conductors of an orchestra in many areas of our work.In the past, repeating simple tasks had meaning as a job. However, these jobs consisted of repetitive tasks only because there were no tools to replace them. Now, even entry-level employees in every company can become supervisors of AI. This will lead to higher productivity. However, humans must develop the ability to evaluate AI-generated work, and higher productivity does not mean less work for humans.I like the following example. Before email, we sent documents by post and waited for them to arrive and for a reply to come back. Physical delivery also required a large workforce. That is no longer the case. Yet if asked whether individual workloads have decreased compared to the past, most of us would say no. I think the same will be true of AI.To emphasize this point again: we can now start our careers as team leaders, with AI as our team members. Previously, moving from team member to team leader required proper evaluation, and those who lacked the qualities of a team leader remained team members. That is no longer the case. People who lack the qualities of a team leader will find it difficult to keep a job, at least in office work. In particular, deep domain knowledge will be an effective means of challenging the judgments of AI.
consensus:
I work in engineering rather than basic science, so I am not certain about this.

As an engineer, however, I see that current AI produces outputs based on the data it has been given (its input).

I believe AI simply scans every possible path and finds the ones that humans have not yet discovered, much like in Where’s Waldo?, where some people can spot him and others cannot.

In addition, unlike humans, AI can integrate knowledge from many different fields and produce new outputs. This is not so much true creation as it is similar to how a person with master’s or doctoral degrees in several fields has a broader view than a doctoral researcher in a single field. Such people can find useful knowledge within existing knowledge, but I do not think they can create something new, even if what they produce appears to be creation.

I hope that applying AI in basic science and other fields will lead to more research outcomes. This will accelerate AI becoming an expert in a wider range of fields and expand the knowledge it receives as input, which will ultimately enable it to produce better answers.

consensus: AI can perform many secondary tasks in research, leaving researchers free to focus on the quality of their work. In my humble opinion, AI has come to empower researchers' work, not limit them. The researcher remains responsible for what they produce, regardless of their tools. future_5_TEXT: I do a lot of chemistry (total organic synthesis) and biology (cell and animal studies) work. Currently, I cannot get AI to perform complex, multi-day syntheses that require multiple machines. When others try to adapt robotic systems to autonomously perform chemistry, they are restricted to reactions that can do not need purification; this approach is catastrophic because we are losing the ability to make chemically diverse compounds. These reasons are why I still need time and people to perform higher-level chemistry.Similarly, autonomous workflows that perform biology work are restricted to questions testable without complexity (e.g. you need to prototype/fabricate a new bioreactor or create a co-culture system where multiple cells are tested together). Again, the reliance of automated, AI-assisted workflows can exhaustively perform these straightforward tasks, and this work is now dominating our field. Unfortunately, this quantity of low complexity research has eroded our ability to design and create systems that answer extremely complex systems.Perhaps AI will help us design complex experiments that we then perform thanks to human flexibility, but I would like to see a human prompt AI to help it design those complex experiments.
consensus:
My community has already adapted by going after quantity, where they generate large quantities of data from simple experimental systems, then use AI to find associations within that data to guide their next steps. But, are those massive, shallow data sets of good enough quality (i.e. were they done because it was convenient and amenable to AI-assisted experimentation, or were they done because they were scientifically correct models)?. 
My hope is that we can use AI and automated workflows to get the first pass multi-parameter (albeit it shallow) data to find new associations that we can then interrogate with lower throughput, careful and rigorous science. I hope AI will let us find and test much more complex hypotheses without the fear that we will waste our time if the idea isn't good (imaging if a PhD project fails because you chose to ask a risky hypothesis). Hopefully the barrier to enter science will be lower and we can bravely ask riskier questions without fear that we'll lose too much time in a failed endeavour. I think science is about taking risks, and methods to reduce the cost of those risks (in time and resources). I'm tired of people asking "safe" questions that are expected to give good results and for people who dare to ask "risky" questions being rejected because failure means a low return on investment (wasted grant money/graduate student time).
comment:
Using AI to solve problems is good if it benefits society. Solving difficult proofs may make safer building designs possible. Finding new correlations in large data sets that lead to a new antibiotic compound would save lives. Those are all good.
But in terms of science, I hope AI will allow us to ask more complicated questions. When the calculator arrived, we could finally do much harder math that let us create better things faster. I hope that AI will be similar; it may help us ask much more complex questions, allowing us to focus our physical human and mental efforts on answering those complex questions. 
In my field, the new heroes are those who use massive screens to create an incredible amount of permutations and then have AI find insights. Those heroes are the ones who can afford those massive screens and computational time. This type of work is now the bar for entry and funding, so we're already seeing biases in funding and publishing opportunities. 
It is important to recognize that people who currently use AI and massive screens are betting that massive data will reveal some insights; this bet is the same someone takes with a lower-throughput and clearly defined hypothesis.
I see two classes here: 
(1) I don't have a scientific hypothesis but will use massive data sets so that AI can help me find one.
(2) I have an idea and will test it, but it might fail. 
I think both are useful and that it is vital that one class starves the other of critical resources.

consensus:
As any other tool, AI is "a good servant, but a wicked master". Adopting the use of AI in scientific research, just as in any other human activity, is an inevitable development. However, accountability for the use of AI has to be rigorous. As a journal editor, I have witnessed several cases of scientific papers submitted to my journal, that were written by AI, without supervision. At first sight, these papers looked good, but after rigorous peer review, it turned out that they were heavily packed with mismatched references, incorrectly interpreted or made-up information, in a way that can only be explained by poor prompting of a LLM and by extensive AI-generated hallucinations. The worst part is that this kind of abuse is not quite readily detectable, even by experienced peer reviewers, and it takes great commitment to bust it. I am worried that this problem (and maybe, other related problems) will become an increasing challenge for the survival of the integrity of scientific research.
I think that the scientific community needs to:
(1) Identify threats from poorly managed AI in scientific research
(2) Identify threats from deliberate abuse of AI tools in scientific research
(3) Develop strategies for proper management of these threats and
(4) Adopt general standards of what is considered an ethical, safe, and responsible use of AI in scientific research.

consensus:
I believe the scientific community should be very cautious about adopting artificial intelligence in scientific research. Although AI may offer certain advantages, I do not agree with relying on it extensively because science should be based on human intelligence, independent thinking, critical analysis and genuine experimental investigation.

In my opinion, scientific research requires researchers to understand their subjects deeply, observe biological processes, analyse findings independently and develop conclusions through their own knowledge and experience. Excessive dependence on AI may weaken these essential research skills and reduce researchers' ability to think critically and creatively.

As a Zoologist with experience in experimental animal research and laboratory investigations, I believe that direct observation, practical laboratory skills and careful interpretation of experimental results are fundamental to scientific discovery. AI cannot replace the experience, judgement and responsibility of a researcher.

I am also concerned about the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated information. AI can produce misleading explanations, incorrect references and biased information, which may affect the quality and credibility of scientific publications if researchers do not verify everything independently.

I believe the scientific community should prioritise human-led research and ensure that AI does not become a substitute for genuine scientific understanding. If AI is used at all, its application should be limited, transparent and carefully evaluated. Researchers must remain responsible for their methods, findings and conclusions.

Overall, I believe scientific progress should be driven primarily by human curiosity, knowledge, critical thinking and experimental evidence. Technology may assist scientific work, but it should never replace the essential intellectual and practical contributions of human researchers.
comment:
I would like to emphasise the importance of maintaining the originality, reliability and integrity of scientific research. In my opinion, scientific progress should always be guided by human curiosity, critical thinking, practical experience and ethical responsibility. Researchers should have the opportunity to develop their own ideas, conduct independent investigations and learn through direct engagement with their research subjects.

I also believe that early-career researchers, particularly those from developing countries, should receive equal opportunities, research facilities and academic support to contribute to the international scientific community. Science should encourage collaboration, knowledge sharing and independent thinking while maintaining high standards of research quality and integrity.
I appreciate the opportunity to share my views and contribute to this discussion. Thank you for considering my perspective.

future_5_TEXT: my long-term strategy has two parts really. first, staying anchored in the intellectual core of my discipline - its central questions, the unresolved tensions, the foundational insights, why it matters at all. as AI makes producing and synthesizing research easier, I think a researcher's value will depend more and more on judgment about what's significant, what's still open, what's worth asking. so I use AI to deepen that engagement, not replace it - it's like an always available partner to synthesize literature, test my arguments, and keep reflecting on the human questions behind the field (what we value, what we're curious about, what we actually need from this kind of knowledge).second, actively strengthening the epistemic communities research depends on - relationships with colleagues at my own university and internationally, built on dialogue, critique and mutual recognition. the human texture of collaborative inquiry shouldn't just survive AI but get stronger with it. and those communities should be the ones setting the direction and judging the value of what we produce with AI, including what AI agents produce on their own, if that's where a discipline goes. AI can expand what we do, but deciding what counts as knowledge and why it matters should stay a shared, human responsibility.
consensus:
I think the community should adapt by doubling down on what makes it a community in the first place. if AI takes on more of the synthesis and production of research, then the real work shifts to collective judgment - deciding what questions matter, what counts as good evidence, what's significant and why. that judgment has always lived in relationships between people - peer review, debate, mentorship, disagreement, mutual recognition - and those need to be strengthened, not thinned out by automation.

concretely that means investing in collaboration across institutions and countries, making space for slower reflective conversations about the core questions of each field, and being explicit about who is accountable for what gets produced with AI (or by AI agents on their own, if a field goes that way). it also means rethinking incentives - if output becomes cheap, counting papers makes even less sense, and we should value depth, critique and the cultivation of good questions. AI can be a powerful partner in all this, but the direction and meaning of science should stay a shared human responsibility.

The scientific community should adapt proactively to recent AI developments by embracing AI as a valuable tool for improving research quality, efficiency and innovation. Researchers should receive appropriate training in artificial intelligence, machine learning, data analytics and digital research methods.

At the same time, scientific institutions should establish clear ethical guidelines to ensure transparency, data privacy, accountability, fairness and reproducibility. AI-generated information, research findings and references must be critically evaluated and scientifically validated by human researchers.

The scientific community should also encourage interdisciplinary collaboration between healthcare professionals, scientists, data analysts and technology experts. Particular attention should be given to using AI to address global health challenges, improve early disease detection, reduce healthcare inequalities and support evidence-based decision-making, especially in low-resource countries.

consensus:
I believe the first step for the scientific community should be to demystify artificial intelligence. Meaningful adaptation cannot happen unless researchers develop a deeper understanding of how these technologies actually work, including their underlying technical principles, capabilities, and limitations.

Much of the current discussion focuses on AI's potential risks, model performance, environmental impact, and ethical implications. While these are important concerns, I believe it is difficult to critically engage with them without first understanding the technology itself. The scientific community should not rely exclusively on the conclusions of AI experts, but should actively promote broader technical literacy and independent critical understanding across disciplines.

In my view, adaptation should begin with education and a genuine effort to understand what AI is, how it operates, what it can and cannot do, and why. Only with this foundation can the scientific community move beyond generalized enthusiasm or skepticism toward a more informed, responsible, and purpose-driven integration of AI into scientific research.

future_5_TEXT: There will always be new technologies and methods that seem to threaten or upset the status quo. AI is another of these. In many respects, the hype around AI tools and LLMs overpromises and overstates the capabilities of these technologies. Like everything else, AI is good for some things and not for others. I am not convinced AI can create new ideas, think critically, write clearly and analytically, and so forth, and no existing evidence has caused me to budge in my opinions here. However, AI can help with structuring writing, coming up with titles, identifying repetitive clauses/paragraphs, debugging code, reformatting in LaTeX very quickly, and doing a rough preliminary bibliographic search. I don't think AI is going to replace researchers, I don't believe AGI is possible, and the idea that AI is or could become conscious seems like a fantasy to me. AI is a terrible editor because it is a terrible writer, and by that I mean "generating sentences that sound nice and are free from typos is not akin to clearly communicating ideas". See: orbital reasoning and sycophancy, too. AI is a terrible peer reviewer because it is not an expert, it fixates on methodological logistics, it cannot imagine new futures or possibilities, and it cannot think or feel or know or learn. So how should we strategise our work in light of recent AI developments? Well, I think the question really ought to be the other way round. Should scientists care about recent AI developments and, if so, why? how? in which fields? where? when? How can we make better decisions about whether, when, and how AI is integrated into science that are based on proven (or provable) outcomes over hype? Why should we change science to put AI into it, rather than change (or limit) AI to, first, preserve and uphold the objectives and principles of science, and then–if and only if AI can help us do science better–determine how to change our working practices accordingly in order to integrate it?
consensus: A major practical concern is the burden on the publishing system. Limiting the number of conference abstracts one can submit is a good start, and something similar could perhaps be implemented for journals. Understanding and educating ourselves on the limitations of AI is another good start. But I think a lot of the challenge is that we simply don't yet know enough.

consensus: The scientific community should actively adapt to AI developments by integrating artificial intelligence into scientific research, education, and innovation. Researchers should be trained to use AI tools for data analysis, bioinformatics, literature reviews, modelling, and scientific discovery. In fields such as genetics, biotechnology, and molecular biology, AI can accelerate genomic analysis, disease research, and the development of new technologies. The scientific community should also establish ethical guidelines to address data privacy, research transparency, bias, and academic integrity. Overall, AI should complement human intelligence and scientific expertise rather than replace researchers.

I think the scientific community needs to shift its focus. AI can increasingly support literature reviews, manuscript writing and peer review, reducing repetitive work. Publishing more papers should no longer be the main goal. Instead, we need to focus on original data, meaningful research questions and independent validation. Retrospective studies should generate hypotheses, followed by prospective studies and randomised trials to demonstrate clinical benefit. We also need to move towards explainable and more autonomous AI systems.

I could also envision a future where publications are accompanied by their complete datasets, allowing researchers to use LLMs to independently analyse the data, challenge conclusions and explore new hypotheses. This would make science more transparent, reproducible and open to scientific debate, while respecting data privacy.

The scientific community must recognize artificial intelligence as a fundamental transformation of research and higher education, rather than simply another technological tool. Universities and research institutions should proactively integrate AI into their research strategies, educational programs, and scientific workflows.

At the institutional level, we must also reconsider how scientific contributions are evaluated, ensuring that innovation, research quality, reproducibility, and responsible AI adoption remain central.

I believe that the future of science lies not in competing with artificial intelligence, but in effectively combining human expertise, creativity, and scientific responsibility with the rapidly expanding capabilities of AI systems. Universities must take a leading role in shaping this transformation.

I think the most important adaptation concerns the incentives for researchers. If the scientific community keeps rewarding volume, researchers will rationally optimize for volume. future_5_TEXT: I consider the LLMs to be similar to a very eager and well meaning first year graduate student.  Someone who wants to impress me with their work and will do a lot.  But they need careful guidance and their work needs careful review.   The LLMs are very helpful assistants.I have adapted my research workflows to allow for the strengths of LLMs to help me take care of tasks that I could not easily do on my own.  For example, I needed to to a literature review that would have required reading about 1,000 abstracts, at the very least, to find manuscripts that needed more detailed reading.  An LLM, instructed to look for specific methods and results, was able to provide me the list of papers I needed to critically review in a few hours.  That has speed up my research by weeks or months.
consensus:
I think we should use LLMs as assistants.  To review papers _before_ submitting to journals.  I'm on an editorial board for a journal and I'm surprised how often I see code and artifacts of LLMs, but the internal consistency of the manuscript is poor as results as simple as sample size are not reported with the same value between abstracts, results, and discussion sections.  An LLM review could help find these minor errors and leave the human review to focus on the science and not the minutia.

Using LLMs and other AI tools as assistants with human oversight can be a huge help to improve research.

We _cannot_ rely on AI to do the work.  My experience has shown that my prompts and the memory of chats with LLMs influence the results that I get.  When I give the exact same prompt to an LLM without a memory of prior chats the results I get are just garbage.
comment:
Data security is a big issues with LLMs and the AIs.   I work with a lot of protected health information that cannot go into an LLM.   So if I ask for help with a research task I can ask generic questions, but that has limited utility.

I have concerns that LLMs are going to reduce collaboration.  In my experience we had two options for collaborative report writing: Microsoft OneDrive or Google Documents.  Google is no longer acceptable as Gemini gets to scoop up drafts and preliminary research.  OneDrive as become difficult to use as one university or another limits access to OneDrive for outside collaborators, or restricts its faculty from accessing another OneDrive instance.  We have stepped backwards towards a document that gets emailed around and then multiple versions have to be reconciled.

future_5_TEXT: First, accept that AI is going nowhere and fighting against the whole concept is futile and senseless. Then, demand and support government and worker union regulations as strongly, visibly and quickly as possible even if it is risky, because purely capitalistic goals will likely lead to a very bleak future quite quickly not just for researchers, but almost all of humanity. This is more important than career safety.From this standpoint, career choices should follow cautious optimism because if regulations do not succeed, there is no point speaking about careers at all. Therefore, I would stay vigilant, understand how LLMs and other AI systems work (not just the marketing-driven buzzwords, but at least some level of technical detail), and based on that assess how they can be safely utilized in my field of work to improve quality and not quantity. If everything goes mostly right, quality should matter a lot more as research quantity becomes more and more meaningless. Furthermore, when using AI tools, try to discover their weaknesses, and importantly, maintain maximal precision when describing the task at hand, do not give over control (you control the project, the AI does some of the heavy lifting, that is how things should be). And one last note: LLMs will only be capable of rapid advancement in fields where the gathering of proof can be fully automated (for now, this is basically mathematics and computer science), in any field requiring more complex physical setup, advancements will be much slower because (in my opinion) LLMs still can not think and reason properly, they just chain experiences together based on a symbolic descriptor knowledge of language (mathematics is a language in this sense) ... they do not know what a tree is, they only know in what context the word tree appears ... if large amounts context is hard to generate in a field because (high number of useless) measurements are slow and expensive, that field is much less likely to experience rapid advancements in AI-based automation.
consensus:
It should adapt quickly. The publish and perish concept was never researcher-friendly, however now the amount (and even impact factor) of publications became almost meaningless. Publications should serve one purpose: communicating ideas and results to the public. If there are other incentives (like grants, job opportunity etc), people will be motivated to publish fabricated or sloppy claims, and with the help of AI, they will do it at an immense speed.
Therefore, frequent physical discussions should form the basis of one's acceptance into the scientific community, not whether they can produce a high amount of figures and words ... I personally already trust a supervisor's opinion on a PhD student far more than their publication record. Furthermore, publication of negative results should be fully accepted. This would help combat fake results, enable the avoidance of already checked useless rabbitholes, and with the help of LLMs a lot more papers could be reviewed.
Also, this is very hypothetical, but if a person or company would be maximum-limited in how many papers they are allowed to publish in a year (let's say, 2 publications per person), they would be naturally inclined to not fake results and in combination with allowing the publication of negative results (instead of marketing-heavy, everything is shiny papers) this would improve paper quality significantly.
comment: This research is very important, please continue. But if possible, do not stop at just publishing the results, try to push for government / EU-level audits on the topic, we need regulations and perspective change in the scientific community, and we need them fast.

I believe that the future of scientific knowledge requires more than technological progress. It requires a renewed understanding of the philosophical foundations of science, including its ontological, epistemological, and axiological dimensions, and the ability to integrate these foundations with the possibilities and challenges of emerging technologies.

Society needs genuine researchers, critical thinkers, and ethically committed intellectuals who can understand these transformations, question established assumptions, and turn meaningful ideas into valuable contributions to humanity.

Equally important, we must reconsider how scientific and intellectual contributions are recognized and rewarded. Society should place greater value on genuine intellectual achievement, scientific integrity, critical thinking, and meaningful contributions rather than allowing visibility, popularity, wealth, or commercial success to become the primary measures of individual worth.

Talented, ethical, and productive individuals should have fair access to the resources, institutional opportunities, and living standards necessary to sustain their intellectual work and contribute to human progress. Scientific excellence should be supported through merit, integrity, and demonstrated contributions, regardless of an individual's social visibility or institutional connections.

Ultimately, technological progress should go hand in hand with intellectual, ethical, and social progress. The purpose of science should remain the advancement of human knowledge and the improvement of society, not merely the acceleration of production or the accumulation of wealth.

future_5_TEXT: How should you strategise about your work for the long term in light of recent AI developments?
consensus: The scientific community should embrace AI as a powerful tool to accelerate scientific progress and improve research productivity. Universities and research institutions should provide researchers with appropriate AI training and encourage the responsible integration of AI into research processes. At the same time, clear guidelines should be established regarding transparency, data integrity, authorship, and accountability. Human researchers should maintain responsibility for evaluating results, ensuring scientific validity, and making important research decisions. Rather than resisting AI, the scientific community should adapt to it while preserving critical thinking, creativity, and scientific independence.
comment: I would encourage the scientific community to explore how AI can be systematically integrated into the research process to improve not only the speed but also the quality and reliability of scientific findings. In particular, AI could be used to identify research gaps, review and synthesize large volumes of scientific literature, improve research methodologies, detect potential errors in data analysis, and help researchers compare alternative models and interpretations. Universities and research institutions could also establish collaborative AI-based research platforms that allow researchers from different disciplines to share knowledge, test hypotheses, and validate findings. Importantly, AI-generated results should always be subject to human evaluation and independent verification to maintain scientific integrity.

In my view, the scientific community should adapt to the development of AI through several key priorities:
1. Move from AI Use to AI Mastery
2. Redefine the Role of Humans in Scientific Research

5. Reduce Inequalities in Access to AI
6. Reform Education and Develop the Next Generation of Researchers
7. Redefine the Value and Competencies of Researchers

The peer review system has been barely functional for a while now (e.g., reports of little depth and poor level of insight from reviewers who didn't commit the time to read the manuscript thoroughly). AI tools could help here if they keep the uploaded data safe (that is, confidential) and don't replace human judgement; for instance, by flagging issues in the form of a condensed report, with the human reviewer being asked to rate the severity of these issues, to suggest possible improvements, and to provide an overall rating and recommendation. Publishers are currently developing tools that work along these lines, and I think the scientific community should adopt these tools.
The training/education of young researchers will have to increasingly focus on explaining the instructive value of performing certain tasks "by hand" rather than automating them using AI tools. I believe that automation has the potential to free researchers from repetitive, routine tasks, giving them more time for deep, creative thought, but we need to maintain the ability to perform all tasks required in our research processes ourselves, at least to be able to competently judge the output of AI tools that we delegate some of these tasks to.

future_5_TEXT: Trying to keep AI use within the boundaries of ethics and true efficiency is incredibly difficult, but crucial for the future. By true efficiency I mean where AI can actually help in a reliable fashion - for example, using AI to screen journal articles for a literature study can seem like a real efficiency boost, but when you have to double check every single summary it gives you because you cannot trust the output then it does not actually save time. Additionally, requiring safeguards from the AI providers is vital, for example privacy safeguards and removal of sycophantic traits from the models, however these are also often not trustworthy, as the constant leaks of information that is supposed to be private show.Another aspect is also that the AI-providers still refuse to give actual costs for the use of their products in terms of energy, water use, emissions etc. This seems ridiculous and should undermine any trust in their use, especially by any organisation which claims to have any care whatsoever for their environmental footprint.

consensus:
We should work more on ethics and integrity - have more dialoge about responsible use of AI and find ways to encourage it.

We should promote ethical use of AI and development of "in house" AI tools  (e.g. developed by Universities) to not be dependent on corporations (to reduce risks like data leaks and exploitations).

We should question different red flags in publishing:
- when someone is producing a too high number of articles per year because in the past it could be a sign of paper mills now it can be related to AI
- when a 1st year PhD student writes a review in very short time
- when a reviewer gives you a review that shows signs of AI, the author should have a chance to question this or report it.

In order to not worry about AI replacing scientists, we should work on more interdisciplinary problems.
Yes, AI could solve tough math problems, but humans are still with the advantage that we have more than just "mathematical brain", we can work in a wet lab, we can recognise feelings/tones in social science research, we have intuition and other capabilities that AI does not have. So it is not about competing with AI, but we need to find ways to use AI wisely and also use our own skills because in this way we can advance faster or more.

Another aspect is also finding the balance between qualitative and quantitative evaluation of scientists and their work - either for projects or for promotions etc. I think it might be problematic to achieve objectivity with qualitative metrics because in science we are in constant competition with each other and if someone will also use AI for qualitative evaluations we might have an additional problem. Yes, quantitative metrics (like IF, h-index, etc.) have their own problems (people cheating, paper mills, etc.), but they had the same measures and objectivity for everyone (if they would play by the rules). In Europe there was a lot of discussion about this transition form quantitative to qualitative evaluation, but there was little changes so far. In this transition AI could be used to help improve the situation or it could lead to more challenges. So we will see have to wait and see.

future_5_TEXT: I currently use AI as a “research mate.” I share my ideas, work in progress and notes, explain which directions seem promising to me and ask specific questions, and then discuss with my AI how to proceed. I have spent a lot of time “educating” my AI by explaining what I find useful and what I expect from a mathematical discussion. I have taught it to be brief, to the point, concrete and critical. This has worked remarkably well for me.Over the past year, I have seen a substantial improvement in the mathematical capabilities of the AI I use. On some technical tasks, such as working through a difficult case or finding a shorter argument, it can already do better than I can. Purely technical, AI seems already to be a better mathematician than I am: quicker, and better at using the right techniques for the problem at hand. I still contribute much of the direction, vision and intuition that guide the work.In the coming years, I expect AI to need much less of that guidance. I think it will become capable of doing independent mathematical research, including identifying promising questions of its own and pursuing them. That could fundamentally change both how we do research and how we measure and value its output. If producing correct results becomes much easier, I think we will place more value on recognising which results matter and on finding proofs that explain why they are true. It will still be our task to check and understand AI’s results and to rewrite and simplify the proofs, often with AI’s help again.
consensus: We should learn how to use AI profitably. Compare it to how chess professionals use the very strong chess programs, to prepare for opponents, finding new possibilities in known openings, study endgames etc. We certainly must learn to work together with AI to make new discoveries, but we must also learn when not to use it, at least initially, to struggle with a problem by ourselves first to build up intuition. But it is hard to predict right now what is going to happen. One thing is sure: we are heading for interesting times, where many of our old mathematical prtoblems will get solved! future_5_TEXT: I am much more driven by the process of research than by its end results. I see research as primarily an exercise in communication between *people*: can we understand complicated natural objects or phenomena? can we explain them to each other? can we build a common understanding of these things? can we establish consensus about how much of this common understanding is grounded in facts versus how much is still hypothetical? can we keep all of this knowledge alive in the minds of practicing scientists, and if so for how long? can we motivate the next generation of people to learn all this and keep it going? All of this requires people talking to people (or writing for people).AI generating scientific results faster than we can read and understand them does not give us much at all (even assuming all these results would be correct and explained in easily understood language). To an extreme, delegating all research to AI means computers writing papers for other computers to read and review. We might get some useful results from this. Particular attention should be paid to protecting vulnerable individuals, preventing algorithmic discrimination, and maintaining transparency in scientific decision-making. The essential challenge is not whether artificial intelligence will transform science, but whether the scientific community can ensure that this transformation remains consistent with human dignity, justice, and academic integrity.

consensus:
I find it difficult to give a definite answer. AI development has not yet reached a clear plateau, and we cannot know whether the measures we propose today will still be appropriate a year from now, or even a few months from now.

For the time being, I believe we have to rely largely on researchers' self-discipline and responsible use of AI, while journal editors and reviewers should focus on identifying research that is genuinely meaningful and valuable.

Academia is already facing increasingly intense and sometimes unhealthy competition. If I choose not to use AI while others do, I may find myself at a significant disadvantage. However, overly strict regulations could also unfairly disadvantage less experienced researchers who are making genuine efforts to conduct independent research.

Therefore, my view is that, until AI development reaches a more stable stage, we should avoid rushing into overly restrictive regulations. Instead, journals should raise their standards for evaluating scientific contributions and focus on identifying and publishing research of genuine value, regardless of whether AI was used in the process.

future_5_TEXT: I believe that the long-term strategy should focus on adapting to AI-driven transformations while preserving and strengthening the intellectual and methodological foundations of my professional expertise. Rather than competing with AI in areas where automation is becoming increasingly efficient, I intend to concentrate on activities where deep domain knowledge, critical thinking, scientific intuition, methodological rigour, and the ability to formulate original research questions remain essential. In my field, this means strengthening the integration of classical zoological and palaeontological expertise with advanced computational methods, statistical analysis, and AI-assisted research.
consensus:
The scientific community should adapt to AI developments proactively, recognising that AI represents not simply another technological tool but a potentially transformative change in the organisation and practice of scientific research. I believe that several aspects deserve particular attention:

- Integration into scientific methodology: AI should become an accepted component of research workflows, facilitating literature analysis, data processing, modelling, statistical analysis, and the exploration of complex datasets. However, its use should remain transparent, reproducible, and subject to independent verification.

- Preservation of scientific standards: The growing ability of AI to generate plausible scientific explanations, references, data interpretations, and even entire manuscripts creates new challenges for research integrity. Scientific institutions and journals should establish clear standards for AI use, authorship, data provenance, validation, and accountability.

- Transformation of scientific education: Researchers should be trained not only to use AI tools but also to understand their underlying principles, limitations, potential biases, and sources of error. Critical thinking and methodological competence will become increasingly important rather than less important.

- Promotion of interdisciplinary research: AI creates opportunities to establish new connections between disciplines, integrate heterogeneous datasets, and investigate phenomena that were previously difficult to analyse. Scientific institutions should encourage this integration while preserving the importance of specialised disciplinary knowledge.

- Protection of intellectual independence: The scientific community should avoid excessive dependence on commercial AI platforms and automated analytical systems. Open-source tools, accessible computational infrastructure, transparent algorithms, and independent scientific expertise should remain important priorities.

I believe that AI should expand the intellectual and methodological capabilities of science rather than replace the human capacity for scientific reasoning. The fundamental principles of science — critical thinking, empirical evidence, methodological rigour, reproducibility, and intellectual independence — should remain unchanged. What should change is our ability to implement these principles more efficiently and explore scientific questions at a scale and complexity that were previously inaccessible.
comment: I am generally positive about the integration of AI into scientific research and recognise its considerable potential. However, I am still trying to determine where the boundaries of its appropriate application should lie: to what extent is the use of AI necessary, desirable, ethically acceptable, or scientifically reasonable? My cautious approach is also partly due to the fact that I have not yet had necessary experience with the most advanced and powerful AI models to develop a comprehensive understanding of their current capabilities and limitations. Therefore, my assessment is still evolving. I believe that identifying the boundaries of appropriate AI use is one of the most important challenges facing the scientific community at the present stage of AI development.

In chatGPT's view, the scientific community should adapt to the use of AI by reviewing how it ensures research reliability and how it trains and evaluates researchers. Four priorities are particularly important:
1. Clarify what researchers should disclose about their use of AI
   Editing English text has different implications for research than analysing data, generating images, or interpreting results. When AI use affects research findings, researchers should document and disclose the tools used, their purpose, how they were used, and how their output was checked.
2. Establish clear expectations for verification and accountability
   Researchers should verify the evidence and validity of AI-generated analyses and interpretations and be able to explain them. Decisions about which tasks to delegate to AI should depend on the potential consequences of errors and how readily the output can be verified.
3. Teach researchers both to use AI and to think and verify independently
   Even when students use AI for assignments, they should be able to explain why they chose a particular method and what the limitations of their results are. Education should also preserve opportunities to develop the subject knowledge and statistical foundations needed to make these judgments.
4. Prioritise quality over quantity in research evaluation
   I expect that, as AI makes it easier to produce papers and analyses, the number of outputs alone will become a less useful measure of research value. Evaluation should place greater emphasis on the importance of the research question, data quality, reproducibility, and meaningful contributions.

future_5_TEXT: My field of research requires a close connection between the production of knowledge and its application in the contexts to which the findings are intended to be transferred. Therefore, my long-term strategy must prioritise both scientific rigour and the usefulness of research in addressing real-world problems.I believe that, even before the rise of AI, research assessment and accreditation systems sometimes favoured the number of publications over their quality, originality or usefulness. Increased scientific output does not always translate into proportional advances in knowledge or improvements in the settings being studied. Frontier research is becoming increasingly scarce and is less valued within the culture of immediate success that researchers face.In this context, I see AI as an opportunity to reduce linguistic and technical barriers and broaden participation among researchers and groups with fewer resources. However, making it easier to publish does not necessarily mean improving research. These tools can also intensify the "publish or perish" dynamic if incentives remain unchanged.For this reason, I want to focus my work on identifying complex problems, formulating relevant questions and developing appropriate methodological designs, including mixed-methods approaches when they offer a better understanding of the problem. I also consider it essential to remain grounded in real-world contexts, so that knowledge transfer and impact help shape research and inform its ongoing development.My strategy is to continue incorporating AI into tasks where it adds value, while retaining responsibility for methodological decisions and the interpretation and verification of results. In the long term, I hope my contribution will be assessed not only by the number of publications I produce, but also by the impact and knowledge transfer achieved through public engagement, citations, innovation projects and broader contributions to society.
consensus:
I believe the scientific community is already adapting to recent advances in AI, for example through policies requiring researchers to disclose its use in publications. However, I think this adaptation should also extend to peer review and the assessment of funding applications, with clear criteria regarding permitted uses, transparency, confidentiality and human accountability.
In my view, the integration of AI should be grounded in methodological rigour and the ability to verify how results were obtained. Journals and funding bodies should therefore strengthen their documentation requirements, including information about which tools were used, for what purposes and how their outputs were verified.
The possibility of generating or manipulating data using AI also makes it necessary to strengthen research traceability. Sharing data, protocols, materials and analysis code can facilitate scrutiny and reproducibility, although their availability alone does not guarantee their authenticity. Synthetic data should be clearly labelled and distinguished from data obtained through observation or experimentation.
Finally, I consider ongoing training essential for researchers and reviewers, so that they can use these tools critically and responsibly while retaining accountability for scientific decisions.

Artificial intelligence has great potential to advance scientific research. However, its development should go hand in hand with ethical responsibility, transparency, and human oversight. AI should support researchers rather than replace human creativity, critical thinking, and scientific judgment.

Nowadays, many people tend to ask AI even simple questions or tasks that they could easily solve on their own, without making an effort to think independently. If this continues, people's critical thinking and ability to conduct independent scientific reasoning may gradually weaken. Scientific and technological progress is certainly valuable, but I believe AI should remain primarily an assistant and a supportive tool, rather than become a substitute for human thinking.

We can already see how dependent many young people and children have become on smartphones and the internet. Some struggle to spend their time or feel comfortable without their devices. We should learn from this experience and avoid developing the same kind of dependence on AI. Technology should help us become more capable, knowledgeable, and creative, not less independent. Ultimately, we must remain in control of technology rather than allow technology to control us.
